## Wind Nacelle (SmartCiti.X · `wind-nacelle`)

**Category:** Energy & Power  
**Trade:** Wind turbine technician  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IBEW / IUOE — utility-scale wind technician; GWO Basic Safety Training (working at height, first aid, manual handling, fire awareness); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 for the rotor, yaw and converter locks; 1910.269 for the electrical isolation  
**Tagline:** Gearbox service ninety metres up: rotor lock, yaw lock, converter isolation, oil sampled hot, brake pads gauged, hatch closed  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Take the turbine work order and the wind limit | Select | Every turbine task carries a wind limit, because above it the nacelle moves, the hatch cannot be controlled and rescue from height stops being possible. The number is on the order and it is checked against the anemometer, not the sky. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Read the nacelle anemometer | Graded reading | Ninety metres up, the wind is not the wind at the base. The nacelle's own anemometer is the one the limit is written against, and it is read at the top before the work starts and again if it freshens. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Three locks: rotor, yaw, converter | Sequence (strict order: rotor lock pin, yaw brake lock, converter isolation) | Three different things can move or energise in here and they are stopped three different ways. The rotor is mechanical, the yaw is hydraulic, the converter is electrical, and one lock does not do the job of the others. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Your lock on the group lock box | Select | The keys to those three locks live in a box that cannot open while your padlock is on it. That is the difference between an isolation somebody else is maintaining and an isolation you control. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Harness, twin lanyard, rated anchor | Sequence (any order: full-body harness, twin lanyard, rated anchor) | Inside a nacelle there is an open hoist hatch and no floor over it. The twin lanyard is so that moving past the hatch never requires being unattached, and the anchor is the one the manufacturer rated, not the nearest pipe. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Open and guard the hoist hatch | Select | The hatch is how the oil and the tools come up, and it is an eighty-five metre hole in the floor for as long as it is open. It gets a rail and it never gets left open unattended. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Check the gearbox oil temperature | Graded reading | Cold oil will not carry the wear particles out and the drain takes an hour. Hot oil comes out as a jet. There is a window between those, and the thermometer says whether you are in it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Set the splash shield | Select | Even inside the window the first of it comes out under head pressure. The shield is between the plug and the person turning it, and it takes two seconds to set. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Crack the drain plug | Turn | Slowly, because a plug that comes out in one turn comes out with the oil behind it. The hose is already connected to the down-tower tank before the plug moves. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Draw the oil sample mid-stream | Select | The first of the flow carries whatever settled in the drain and the last carries the sump floor. The mid-stream sample is the one that represents the oil the gearbox has actually been running on. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Gauge the yaw brake pads | Graded reading | The yaw brake is what holds the nacelle against a wind shift. Pads below the limit let the nacelle walk under load, and a nacelle that walks tears the tower cable loop it is hanging on. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Refit and torque the drain plug | Timed hold | A gearbox drain plug backing out is eight hundred litres of oil down a tower and a machine destroyed. New washer, right figure, held to the click. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Walk the nacelle before you close it | Find (any order: chafed converter cable, loose coupling guard) | The next person up this tower might be six months away. What gets written down today is what gets fixed before the machine finds it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `unlocked-rotor` | You opened the gearbox with the rotor lock pin not seated. A parked rotor still creeps in gusting wind, and a turning low-speed shaft inside a nacelle takes an arm before anyone can react. The pin goes in and is confirmed visually, every time. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `yaw-free` | You are working with the yaw drive free. The nacelle will hunt into a wind shift with you standing in it, and the tower cable below you twists with it — a yaw event with the hatch open throws tools out and drops them ninety metres. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `unclipped` | You moved inside the nacelle without transferring your lanyard. There is an open hatch in this floor and an eighty-five metre drop under it; the twin lanyard exists so that one end is always attached during the transfer. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `hot-oil` | You cracked the drain at full operating temperature with no shield. Gear oil at ninety degrees under head pressure comes out as a jet, not a trickle, and it goes straight through a coverall. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Transformer Vault (SmartCiti.X · `transformer-vault`)

**Category:** Energy & Power  
**Trade:** Substation / underground distribution electrician  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IBEW — underground distribution journeyman; NFPA 70E arc-flash boundary and PPE category; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.269 for the switching, clearance and grounding; ASTM D3612 dissolved-gas sampling  
**Tagline:** Padmount switching under a written order: clearance, hot stick, load-break elbows, grounds applied, oil drawn for DGA  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Take the written switching order | Select | Underground loops can be fed from either end. The order says which switch opens first so the vault is fed from nowhere, and it is written down because a switching sequence held in the head is how a loop gets backfed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Arc-rated PPE and the flash boundary | Sequence (any order: arc-rated suit, dated class 2 gloves, flash boundary markers) | The label on the transformer gives the incident energy and the boundary. The suit is chosen against that number, the gloves are in test date, and the boundary keeps everyone who is not switching outside it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Open and ventilate the vault | Select | A below-grade vault is a permit space. Whatever has collected in it — SF6, exhaust, water vapour off a hot tank — sits at the bottom where a person's head goes first. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Test the vault atmosphere | Graded reading | The meter goes down before the person does, and it reads at the bottom, not at the lip. Twenty point nine oxygen at the top of a vault says nothing about the bottom of it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Open the loop switch to the order | Turn | The loop is opened at the point the order specifies so that the section containing this transformer is fed from neither direction. Opening the wrong end leaves it live from the other. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Park the load-break elbows with the hot stick | Timed hold | A load-break elbow interrupts current as it breaks, which is violent and bright. The stick keeps the length of an insulated pole between that event and the person making it, and the elbow goes on a parking stand rather than lying in the vault. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Test dead on every phase | Graded reading | The tester is proved on a known live source before and after, because a tester that has failed reads dead on everything. Three phases, every time — the one you skip is the one that is still up. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Apply the grounds — earth end first | Sequence (strict order: ground cluster to the grid, phase A, phase B, phase C) | The earth connection is made before the phase connection, every time. Making the phase end first turns the ground set into the conductor that carries fault current through your hands to nothing. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Take your clearance | Select | The clearance is held by the person doing the work, not by the control room's intention. The number on the tag matches the number on the order, and it comes off when the work does. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Draw an oil sample for dissolved-gas analysis | Graded reading | Dissolved-gas analysis reads the transformer's health from what the oil has absorbed — acetylene means arcing, ethylene means overheating. Air in the syringe invalidates the sample, so it is drawn with no bubble. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Remove the grounds — phases first, earth last | Sequence (strict order: phase C, phase B, phase A, ground cluster last) | Coming off, the earth connection is the last thing broken, for the same reason it was the first thing made. Anything else leaves a ground set hanging on a conductor with no path to earth. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Walk the vault before you close it | Find (any order: cracked standoff bushing, oil stain under the tank) | The vault gets opened once a year if it is lucky. What you noticed today is what gets fixed before the next fault finds it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `bare-elbow` | You went for the elbow bare-handed. A 600-amp load-break elbow is an energised connector behind an insulating boot — it is pulled with a hot stick, in rubber gloves, from outside the flash boundary, and never with a hand on the cable. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `no-ground-work` | You started work on the conductor before the grounds were applied. De-energised is not the same as grounded: a backfeed from a customer generator or an induced voltage from the parallel circuit will kill you just as dead, and the grounds are the only thing that holds the conductor at earth. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `vault-entry` | You climbed into the vault before it was tested and ventilated. Below grade with a transformer in it is a permit space — heavier-than-air gases pool in it, and an oil fire consumes the oxygen in seconds. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `wet-gloves` | Those rubber gloves have been sitting in the rain in an open bag. Class 2 gloves are tested, dated and kept in their bag dry; wet or undated gloves are not PPE, they are the illusion of it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

# Mobility & Transit

## Signal Cabinet (SmartCiti.X · `signal-cabinet`)

**Category:** Mobility & Transit  
**Trade:** Traffic signal technician  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IBEW — IMSA Level II Traffic Signal Technician certified  
**Tagline:** Intersection work zone, controller fault diagnosis and conflict monitor integrity  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Notify the traffic management centre | Select | The centre is watching this intersection remotely through the same detector loops you are about to work on. If they see it drop without warning, dispatch reads it as an outage rather than a scheduled repair and sends a second crew straight into the work zone you have not set up yet. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Set the work zone | Sequence (any order: advance warning sign, taper cone, buffer cone, arrow board) | Traffic needs to be told what is happening far enough back to react to it, which is exactly what the temporary-traffic-control layouts in Part 6 of the MUTCD are built around. The advance sign gives a driver time to notice, the taper is what actually moves them over, and the buffer is what absorbs the one who does not. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | High-visibility clothing | Select | You are a pedestrian in a roadway with a controller cabinet between you and oncoming traffic. Conspicuity, the class-3 garment rated for this kind of exposure, is the only protection you have against a driver who is looking at their phone instead of the cones. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Open the controller cabinet | Turn | Now that the zone is up and the centre knows, the cabinet can come open — with the door swung out to put a sheet of steel between you and the running lane, not swung back flat because that makes the rack easier to reach. The door is the only physical barrier at head height you have once you are working inside, and which way it faces is a decision you make once and live with for the whole job. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Put the intersection into flash | Select | Flash puts the intersection into a known, fail-safe state every driver recognises on sight. Working a running controller means one wrong card pull changes a phase under a car that is already committed to the intersection at 50 km/h. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Find the cabinet faults | Find (any order: scorched load switch, corroded ground bond, loose detector loop terminal) | Fault-finding is looking, not swapping — an IBEW-trained signal tech reads the rack the way NECA apprenticeship training teaches it: scorching, corrosion and a backed-out conductor each tell you a different part of the story, and none of them is fixed by trading a healthy part for another healthy part. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Replace the failed load switch | Select | A welded load switch can hold an output on regardless of what the controller commands it to do. Contacts that have arced together do not get reset back into service — they get replaced, because the next command they ignore could be the one that drops a conflicting phase. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Test the conflict monitor | Graded reading | The malfunction monitoring unit watches for conflicting greens on the same intersection and forces the whole thing to flash the instant it sees one. Proving it trips inside its rated window, not just that it powers up, is the entire reason the intersection is allowed back in normal service today. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Set the clearance interval | Graded reading | Clearance timing is calculated from this approach's posted speed and the intersection's width, not chosen by feel. Shave it to improve throughput and you build a dilemma zone: a band of distance where a driver can neither stop in time nor clear the box before opposing traffic gets its green. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Return the intersection to normal | Timed hold | You watch it cycle before you pack up, start to finish, phase by phase, and you stay on the switch the whole time so the intersection can be put straight back into flash the instant something is wrong. A controller that comes back with the wrong phase order, a stuck call or a detector that never drops is your fault until you have personally seen it run one complete, correct cycle with your own eyes. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Recover the work zone | Carry and place | The zone comes down from the traffic side inward — arrow board last out of the lane, not first — so at every point in the teardown you are never the first unprotected thing an approaching driver meets, the way you were on the way in. The board itself is the heaviest thing in the kit and the one that gets walked across a live lane if nobody has thought about where it is going before they start moving it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `conflict-bypass` | That jumper defeats the conflict monitor. The monitor is the only thing that stops the controller showing green to crossing traffic at the same time. Defeating it is how intersections kill people. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `live-terminals` | You are across the 120 V field terminals with the cabinet live. Those feed the heads outside; the cabinet stays powered even in flash, which is exactly the kind of exposure NFPA 70E's electrical safe work practices are written to control. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `step-into-road` | You stepped into the running lane. Your work zone exists so you never have to — stay behind the cones and let traffic pass. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `service-disconnect` | That is the utility service disconnect on the pole, ahead of the cabinet's own breaker. Everything on the line side of it stays energised no matter what you switch off inside the cabinet, and it is not the signal technician's to open — the utility owns that point of connection and works it with their own clearance. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `ladder-unsecured` | That ladder is footed on a kerb, unsecured, beside a live lane. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.23 requires it set on a level, stable base and secured against displacement before anyone climbs it — signal heads get accessed from a properly set and footed ladder or not at all. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Flight Deck (SmartCiti.X · `flight-deck`)

**Category:** Mobility & Transit  
**Trade:** Drone / UAS ground technician  
**Certification / standard claimed:** Teamsters — FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate holder  
**Tagline:** Vertiport ramp safety: rotor lockout, battery handling, autonomous route planning and pre-flight release  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Check the flight authorization | Select | Airspace and ramp status change by the hour under 14 CFR Part 107 small-UAS operating rules. Working under an aircraft that the fleet scheduler expects to be flying at 14:20 is how a ground crew ends up standing under a live approach with no warning it is coming. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Set the ground safety zone | Sequence (any order: cone at the ramp edge, cone at the taxi line, ramp barrier) | The zone keeps bystanders off an active ramp and keeps you inside a boundary the flight controller's automated landing logic actually respects — the same OSHA ramp-safety logic that applies to ground crews under any aircraft, crewed or not. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Disarm the flight controller | Select | Disarmed means the motors cannot spin regardless of what a stray signal, a bumped stick or a fleet scheduler's queued mission commands them to do. Nothing touches the airframe before this is confirmed on the link, not assumed from how quiet the rotors look. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Fit the rotor locking pins | Select | Disarmed is a software state that a dispatcher in an office can silently overwrite; the pin is physical and nobody can push a firmware update through it. Both together, not either alone, are what makes an accidental spin-up impossible instead of merely unlikely. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Complete the pre-flight inspection | Find (any order: chipped propeller, cracked motor arm, obstructed obstacle sensor) | A pre-flight inspection is a search, not a checklist tick, and it is the finding the incident report reads first if the release goes ahead without it. Damage that looks cosmetic sitting on the ramp is structural the moment it is loaded at altitude. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Replace the damaged propeller | Carry and place | Matched, balanced propellers keep the airframe's vibration profile inside what the flight controller expects from its accelerometers. A chipped blade throws that profile off just enough that the controller starts compensating for damage instead of flying the mission. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Inspect and fit the flight battery | Select | The battery bay is the last thing on the airframe that opens, and only after the aircraft cannot spin a motor even if you drop a tool into it. A swollen LiPo cell is already venting internally, and NFPA's guidance on lithium battery hazards treats that as a fire risk the instant it is found, not a defect to fly around. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Verify cell voltage balance | Graded reading | A pack with one cell drifting low will sag under load exactly when the aircraft needs full power to land, not while it is cruising at altitude with margin to spare. Balance is checked before every single flight, not just at charge time when the pack was last on the bench. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Contain the damaged battery | Select | A venting lithium cell in a normal storage bin can ignite everything stacked around it within seconds. The fireproof bag, the same NFPA-recommended containment used across the trade for damaged lithium packs, buys the minutes it takes to get it somewhere it can vent safely. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Remove the rotor pins | Select | The pins are the last thing an IAM-trained ground technician does at the aircraft itself. Everything after this — the route, the upload, the verification — happens at the console, so nothing puts a hand near the airframe again between the pins coming out and the release being signed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Plan the autonomous delivery route | Sequence (strict order: launch waypoint, relay waypoint, delivery waypoint) | The flight controller flies the waypoints in the exact order they were entered, not the order that looks correct on the map. Swap the relay and the delivery point and the aircraft plans a straight line through restricted airspace instead of the corridor around it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Upload the mission | Select | A planned route sitting on the tablet is not a flight plan yet — it is a drawing. Uploading it is the step that actually replaces whatever the aircraft was flying before with the route you just built and checked. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Verify the route against restricted airspace | Timed hold | Airspace restrictions shift by the hour under Part 107 operating rules, so a corridor that was clear when the route was drawn an hour ago may not be clear now. You verify the specific route you are about to fly, every single time, not the general area it happens to pass through. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Sign the pre-flight release | Select | The release is a signed record that one named, IAM-certified technician personally checked specific things on this specific airframe today. It is the document an incident investigation reads first if something goes wrong in the air twenty minutes from now. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `spinning-rotor` | You reached toward a rotor with the flight controller still armed. A carbon propeller at flight RPM will not stop for a hand — the aircraft is disarmed and the props are pinned before anyone approaches. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `swollen-battery` | That battery pack is swollen. A puffed LiPo cell is already venting internally; charging or flying it is how a ramp fire starts. It goes straight into the fireproof containment bag. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `ramp-incursion` | You crossed into the active approach path while an aircraft is inbound. The ramp boundary exists because a returning drone is looking for a clear landing pad, not for a person standing on it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `damaged-prop` | That propeller has a chip out of the leading edge. A damaged prop at altitude changes its balance and can shear — it is swapped before the aircraft goes anywhere. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Track Access (SmartCiti.X · `track-access`)

**Category:** Mobility & Transit  
**Trade:** Rail track worker  
**Certification / standard claimed:** BMWED — FRA 49 CFR 214 Roadway Worker Protection qualified  
**Tagline:** Track possession, third-rail isolation and lookout protection  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Attend the possession briefing | Select | Everyone on site works to the same plan under FRA roadway worker protection rules at 49 CFR Part 214. A worker who missed the briefing does not know where the protection actually starts and ends, and the crew has no way to know that they do not know. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Take possession from the signaller | Select | Until the signaller says the words that grant it, the section is still open to traffic as far as the signalling system is concerned, regardless of what the engineering schedule says should be happening. Possession is a spoken confirmation you can quote back, not an assumption drawn from a timetable. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Isolate the traction current | Turn | The isolator is what removes the current, but the switch position alone is not proof of anything — that comes at the next step. It goes fully over, too: a lever left part way across its travel is a lever that has not actually broken the circuit, whatever the handle looks like from the cab. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Prove the traction rail is dead | Graded reading | The same rule as any other isolation: measured with an approved tester, never assumed from a switch position or a control-room readout. Seven hundred volts DC through a conductor rail gives no warning and needs no arc to kill, so a reading near zero is the only thing that makes the rail approachable at all. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Mark the limits of possession | Sequence (any order: limit of possession board — up end, limit of possession board — down end) | The boards are the only thing a train crew, a signaller or another gang can actually see from a moving vehicle that marks where your protection begins and ends — everything past a board is a section that still runs to normal rules. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Post the lookout | Select | The lookout's only job is watching the line in both directions and giving a warning early enough for the gang to clear it, coordinated the same way a SMART-represented train crew coordinates a move through a work zone. Sighting distance is calculated back from line speed, not chosen for convenience. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Fit the rail bonding clamp | Select | The bond maintains the signalling circuit's continuity across the joint you are about to work on, so the interlocking upstream still sees an occupied or clear track correctly instead of losing the detection the moment the rail is broken. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Measure track gauge | Graded reading | Standard gauge is held to a tight tolerance for a reason: outside it, a wheel flange stops following the rail head and starts climbing it under load, which is how a slow, boring maintenance defect turns into a derailment nobody saw building. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Replace the defective fastener | Carry and place | A loose fastener lets the rail move under load, and the failure is progressive: a little play becomes a lot of play as every axle passing over it works the hole a fraction wider. Fixed now, with the seat clean and the new fastener carried across and seated square, it is a five-minute job. Missed, or set crooked because it was rushed, it is a derailment risk that starts as a barely audible click under a slow-moving inspection car. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Walk the site for anything left behind | Find (any order: wrench left on the ballast) | A tool left on the track is a foreign object under the next train — caught in a set of points it derails a movement, and lying on the running rail it becomes a projectile under a wheel at line speed. The tally is counted out and counted back against the list every time, but the list only catches what somebody actually walked the site to find; it does not walk itself. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Restore traction current | Select | Confirmed clear of the rail, then and only then re-energised. The sequence never reverses. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Hand possession back | Select | The section stays under your protection until you formally hand it back. Walking away without the call is how a possession never actually closes. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `third-rail` | That is the traction current rail. Isolation confirmed elsewhere does not matter here until you have proven this section dead — it carries enough current to kill on contact, no arc required. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `unprotected-crossing` | You crossed the running line without the lookout's clearance. A train at line speed covers that distance faster than you can react to a warning. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `solo-worksite` | You are working without a second person in sight. Track protection is never a one-person job — the lookout exists because you cannot watch the line and do the work at the same time, and an ANSI/ISEA-rated hi-vis vest does nothing for a worker that nobody is actually watching for. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `unmarked-boundary` | That limit of possession has no board. Without a marked boundary a train movement has no way to know where your protection actually ends. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Bus Depot Lift (SmartCiti.X · `bus-depot-lift`)

**Category:** Mobility & Transit  
**Trade:** Transit bus technician — electric fleet  
**Certification / standard claimed:** ATU / IAM — ASE Transit Bus (H series) with H8 EV / hybrid-electric; ALI Lifting It Right (ANSI/ALI ALOIM); OSHA 1910.147 lockout for high-voltage disable  
**Tagline:** Electric bus on column lifts: HV disable and prove, chocks, pad placement, synchronised raise, locks down, under-bus work, controlled lower  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the repair order and the lift points | Select | Every model lifts at different frame points and disables its high-voltage system a different way — a point that is correct on a diesel cousin can be sheet metal on this one. The diagram and the disable procedure for this specific bus are read before anything is touched. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Disable the high-voltage system | Sequence (strict order: master switch, HV service disconnect) | The service disconnect opens the traction battery circuit itself, not just the low-voltage control loop the master switch runs. It is pulled after the master switch, in that order, and it stays in your pocket so nobody can reinsert it while you are underneath a bus you believe is de-energised. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Prove the HV bus is de-energised | Graded reading | The traction battery's capacitors hold a lethal charge for a period after the disconnect is pulled, following the same live-dead-live discipline NFPA 70E requires of any electrical energy source. The meter, read only after the full wait, is the actual proof the orange cables are safe to touch. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Chock the wheels | Sequence (any order: front chocks, rear chocks) | The bus must not roll on the lift pads during the first few inches of travel, when the columns have barely started to take the load and the pads have the least purchase on the frame. Chocks at both axles and the parking brake set before any column moves at all. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Place the lift pads on the frame points | Carry and place | The frame lift point is engineered by the manufacturer to carry the full weight of an 18-tonne bus; nothing else along that frame or body is. The pad goes exactly on the marked point, on every column, with no column left to guesswork. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Raise in sync | Tracked hold | Four columns raising even slightly unevenly twist the bus's frame and shift its whole load onto only two of the four pads. The controller works to sync them, but the technician watches the level readout the entire climb and stops the raise the moment one column leads. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Lower onto the mechanical locks | Timed hold | The bus is worked under only once it is resting on its mechanical locks, not on the columns' hydraulic rams. Lowering onto the locks takes the load off the hydraulics entirely, so a seal or a hose failure afterward has nothing left under it to drop. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Work under the bus | Select | Everything before this step — HV proven dead, chocks set, pads on the frame, locks engaged — is what turns pulling a drive motor from underneath an 18-tonne bus into an ordinary task instead of a gamble. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Inspect under the bus while it is up | Find (any order: chafed HV cable jacket) | A bus sits up on locks with clear access underneath for maybe an hour a month, and that hour is the only chance anyone gets to actually see the underside. What gets caught now is what keeps this bus out of the shop again next month. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Clear the bay and lower | Select | The lower is called only by the person who has personally looked underneath the bus and confirmed the bay is clear of hands, tools and feet. The service disconnect goes back in only once the bus is back down on the ground and the job is fully closed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `under-hydraulic` | You went under the bus with the columns still on hydraulics, locks not engaged. A seal, a hose or a valve is all that is holding 18 tonnes over you; the mechanical locks are what a person works under. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `hv-bare` | You touched the orange high-voltage cable with bare hands before the system was disabled and proven. The traction battery is 600 V and does not care that the bus is switched off. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `pad-on-body` | You put a lift pad on the body skirt instead of the frame lift point. The skirt is sheet metal; it crushes, the bus shifts on the columns, and it comes down where it likes. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `raise-no-chock` | You started the raise with the wheels unchocked and the bus in neutral. A bus that rolls on the pads as it lifts rolls off them. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Airport Ramp (SmartCiti.X · `airport-ramp`)

**Category:** Mobility & Transit  
**Trade:** Airline ramp agent / ground handler  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IAM and Transport Workers Union ramp locals; IATA Ground Operations Manual (AHM 630 ground support equipment, ERA safety envelope); FAA 14 CFR 139.303 personnel training and 139.329 movement-area safety; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178 for powered ramp equipment; ANSI/ISEA 107 high-visibility apparel for anyone on the movement area  
**Tagline:** Gate turn: FOD walk and equipment restraint line, marshal onto the lead-in, chocks before anything touches it, cones set, ground power and headset to the flight deck, bridge to the door, loader at walking pace, all-clear only when chocks and cones are back  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the turn plan | Select | Stand geometry and the aircraft type on the turn plan decide where the chocks and cones actually go and how far the bridge has to travel to reach the door, none of which can be worked out once the aircraft is already on the stand. Under IATA's AHM 630 ground-operations guidance, the turn is planned on the ground before the aircraft is even on final approach. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Walk the stand for FOD | Find (any order: loose bolt on the stand, cargo strap on the lead-in line) | Foreign object damage is the single most expensive avoidable event on a ramp — one bolt through an intake writes off an engine, and a strap wrapped around a nose gear can bring an aircraft to a stop on the lead-in line. The walk happens before every single arrival regardless of how clean the stand looked last time, and what is found goes in the bin, never kicked aside for someone else to deal with. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Stage behind the line | Sequence (any order: equipment restraint line clear, ground equipment behind the line, hi-vis and ear protection) | Until the aircraft is fully stopped and chocked, the equipment restraint line is the entire boundary between the ramp crew and a moving aeroplane the pilot cannot see past its own wingtips. Everyone and everything stays behind it, brakes set on the ground equipment and the crew in hi-vis with hearing protection on, per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178 for the powered equipment already staged there. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Marshal the aircraft in | Tracked hold | From the flight deck of a narrow-body, the pilot cannot see the nosewheel, the wingtips, or anything directly in front of the aircraft for the last stretch of the approach. The marshaller standing on the lead-in line, with steady wands and a steady walking rate, is the only reference the flight crew has for closing the final thirty metres onto the stand. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Stop on the mark | Graded reading | The stop bar marking is calibrated for exactly one aircraft type on that stand: it is the one point where the jet bridge actually reaches the door and the wingtip still clears the adjacent stand's equipment. Stop a metre long or a metre short of that mark and one of those two things is no longer true, and neither is something the crew can fix after the aircraft is parked. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Chock and cone | Sequence (strict order: nose gear chocks, main gear chocks, wingtip and engine cones) | Chocks before any contact is the rule the whole ramp runs on, because until they are set nothing except the flight crew's own brakes is holding a parked aircraft on a stand that is rarely perfectly level. The cones at the wingtips and the engine mark the exact parts of the aircraft that a reversing tug or a swinging loader must never find with a mirror. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Ground power and headset | Sequence (any order: ground power connected, headset to the flight deck) | Ground power connected first is what lets the engines and the auxiliary power unit actually shut down without losing electrics on the flight deck. The headset plugged into the nose interphone is the only direct line to the flight deck for the rest of the turn, and it is the same connection pushback will eventually happen on, so it is tested now rather than assumed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Drive the bridge to the door | Tracked hold | A jet bridge driven fast into an aircraft door is a hull strike, and a hull strike on a narrow-body does not just delay this turn — it grounds the aircraft for inspection and cancels the next several flights on its rotation. Bringing it in steadily, watching the cab height against the door sill with the auto-level following, is what keeps the canopy from ever making first contact at speed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Align and dock the bridge | Graded reading | The bridge's canopy has to seal against the fuselage skin around the door, and the auto-level system keeps the cabin sill matched to the bridge floor as the aircraft physically rises on its gear while cargo and passengers come off. Docked off-centre, the seal leaks weather into the jetway and the sill develops a step that becomes a trip hazard for every passenger who crosses it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Bring the belt loader to the hold | Carry and place | Every vehicle that approaches a parked aircraft on the ramp does it at walking pace and stops short of the skin, under the same AHM 630 ground-support discipline that governs everything else on this turn. The last metre to the fuselage is closed with the loader's own platform, never by rolling the vehicle itself the rest of the way in. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Clear the stand and give the all-clear | Sequence (strict order: cones back on the truck, chocks pulled, all-clear to the flight deck) | The cones come up first, the chocks second to last, and the all-clear last of all, given with the chocks held up in plain view of the flight deck. That specific sequence and that visible signal are the pilot's only proof, from inside a cockpit that cannot see the nosewheel, that nothing ground crew placed is still attached to or under their aircraft before they move it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `cross-engine-arc` | You walked through the engine's intake arc with the engine turning. A running narrow-body engine ingests a person from several metres in front of it, and the exhaust behind it will blow a baggage cart across the ramp. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `vehicle-past-line` | You drove ground equipment past the equipment-restraint line before the aircraft stopped and was chocked. Every year a piece of ground equipment strikes a moving aircraft on a ramp; the line exists to make that impossible. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `chock-pulled-early` | You pulled the chocks with the bridge still on the aircraft. Nothing holds the aircraft then except its brakes, and a brake release with the bridge attached takes the door off. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `under-fuselage-loading` | You stood under the fuselage while the loader was moving against it. The loader's platform is a shear point against the aircraft skin, and there is no room to get out from under it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## RCL Switching (SmartCiti.X · `rcl-switching`)

**Category:** Mobility & Transit  
**Trade:** Remote control locomotive operator / switchman  
**Certification / standard claimed:** SMART Transportation Division and BLET — the carrier's remote control locomotive operator certification, over conductor and engineer certification under FRA 49 CFR 242 and 240; 49 CFR 218 Subpart B blue signal protection of workers; 49 CFR 232 brake system standards, including the securement of unattended equipment  
**Tagline:** A remote control shove worked from the ground: point protection on every movement, a blue signal put up and taken down by the one hand it protects, three-step before anybody fouls the equipment, and securement proved by pulling against it  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Take the job briefing and the switch list | Select | A remote control job is worked from the ground by one person with the whole movement in their hands, so the plan is settled before the wheels turn. The briefing is also where the crew agrees who holds the point and who is being protected, and that is the one thing nobody can work out later by looking. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Belt the box on, link it, prove its safeties | Sequence (strict order: operator control unit and harness, link the box to the locomotive, prove the tilt and vigilance features) | The box on your chest is the cab now, and it is the only cab. Linking it is what hands a locomotive to somebody standing on the ballast, and the features that stop the movement when the operator goes down get proved at the start, while proving them costs nothing but a minute. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Prove the brakes answer the box | Graded reading | Everything after this depends on the movement stopping when a hand that is not in the cab tells it to. The reduction is read off a gauge rather than assumed from a button, because a link that talks to a locomotive is not the same thing as a link that brakes it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Take the point before anything moves | Select | This is the rule the whole job hangs on: the movement goes no further than the operator can see it stop. On a shove that means being ahead of the leading end, on the side the track is visible from, and it means taking that position first rather than catching up with it afterwards. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Shove at a speed you can stop within half of what you can see | Tracked hold | Half the range of vision, short of anything fouling the track, is point protection written as a number. It is not a fixed speed — it is the speed at which this much clear track is enough, so it comes down when the sight line shortens and it comes down to zero when the sight line closes. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Line the hand switch and look at the points | Turn | The target on a switch stand tells you what the handle did, not what the points did. A point that has not seated leaves a gap for a wheel to pick, and the only way that gets found before a derailment is somebody walking up and looking at the rail. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Couple at coupling speed | Graded reading | Cars are coupled slowly because the impact carries on through the lading, the draft gear and whatever is standing at the far end of the track. A hard joint is also how a cut somebody thought was secured ends up shoved out the other end. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Set three-step protection and hold for the acknowledgement | Timed hold | Three-step is the machine's undertaking that it cannot move: brakes applied, reverser centred, power off. On a remote control job the same person asks for it and then relies on it, which is exactly why it is held until the acknowledgement comes back rather than assumed from a button press. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Display your own blue signal | Select | A blue signal is personal. The worker it protects is the one who displays it and the only one who may remove it, and while it is up the equipment is not coupled to and is not moved by anybody. That is what makes it worth more than an arrangement with whoever happens to be on duty. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Change the broken knuckle | Carry and place | This is the work all that protection was set for, and the reason it has to be personal: the person whose arms are inside the coupler is the person who asked for three-step and put the blue signal up. Knuckles are also heavy and awkward, which is its own argument for not doing this twice. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Wind the hand brake down on the cut | Turn | A cut left standing is held by hand brakes, not by air, because air leaks off and nobody will be here when it does. How many brakes and how hard is a judgement about the grade, the tonnage and the wind — and it is a judgement that gets tested in the next step rather than trusted. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Prove the securement by pulling against it | Graded reading | Securement is verified by attempting to move the equipment, not by counting turns on a wheel. A wheel that span freely because the chain was slack feels exactly like a wheel that took up — right up until the cut is found somewhere nobody left it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Check the cut is standing in the clear | Select | Equipment left fouling the next track is the cause of the side-swipe nobody saw coming, and it is always a car end sticking out by a couple of feet at a spot the operator never walked to. The clearance point is marked so that it can be looked at instead of estimated from down the yard. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Walk the cut before you leave it | Find (any order: dragging air hose, loose handhold) | Nobody else is walking this cut tonight. Defects on yard equipment get found by the last person who worked it, walking it with their eyes open, and the list of what gets missed is the same list every time: hoses, handholds, sill steps and brake rigging. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 15 | Take your own blue signal down, last | Select | It comes down by the same hand that put it up, and it comes down last, after the work is done and the people are clear. A blue signal taken down by somebody else, or taken down early because the track is wanted, is the precise failure the rule was written for. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `lost-sight` | You kept shoving with the leading end behind the standing cut on the next track. Point protection is not a speed limit, it is a promise that the movement can be stopped short of whatever is in front of it — and that is not a promise anybody can make about track they cannot see. When the leading end goes out of sight, the movement stops until it is back in sight or somebody else has the point. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `ride-the-shove` | You stepped onto the side ladder of a car that is moving. Getting on and off moving equipment is how switchmen lose feet, and on a remote control job it is worse than that: the operator riding the car is the operator who has stopped watching the leading end, and the only brake that cut has is the box on your chest. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `between-cars` | You went in between equipment that is neither separated nor protected. A cut with a locomotive coupled to it can move, and it does not need anybody to make a mistake first — slack running in will close a gap you are standing in faster than you can get out of it. Nothing goes between until the equipment is separated, protected, and protected by you. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `over-the-coupler` | You climbed over the drawbar to get to the other side. Crossing over couplers and drawbars puts your whole body in the one place on a car that closes under slack, and it is the crossing people make without thinking because the alternative is a long walk round the end. Go round the end, far enough out that nothing can reach you. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

# Water & Environmental

## Valve Vault (SmartCiti.X · `valve-vault`)

**Category:** Water & Environmental  
**Trade:** Water utility operator  
**Certification / standard claimed:** LIUNA — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 permit-required confined space entrant; ANSI/ASSP Z117.1 confined spaces; NIOSH confined-space entry criteria  
**Tagline:** Permit-required confined space entry: isolation, atmosphere, roles and retrieval  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Open the entry permit | Select | The permit is the record that this particular vault, on this particular day, has already been checked against every item 1910.146 requires before a cover comes off a footway — the isolation point on the main, the reading the atmosphere has to hold, who is standing where, and how somebody gets pulled back out through an opening barely wide enough for their shoulders. Nobody works off what the last crew did in a different vault; the paper in hand is the only one that counts today. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Guard the opening | Sequence (any order: cone upstream, cone downstream, hatch guard rail) | A footway with an open manhole in it is a hazard to the public long before it is a hazard to the crew — a jogger, a stroller, someone reading a phone screen instead of the pavement. The cones turn foot traffic wide of the kerb and the rail closes off the last few feet around the hatch, and both go up before the cover is lifted, not after somebody has already wandered up to the edge to see what the crew is doing. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Assign the entry roles | Sequence (strict order: entry supervisor, attendant, entrant) | A permit space assigns its three roles top down for a reason that has nothing to do with rank: the supervisor is the one person whose sign-off says the isolation, the atmosphere and the rescue plan have actually been checked, and that judgment has to exist before anyone is posted to watch the hatch or handed a harness. Naming an entrant first and sorting the rest out afterward is how a crew talks itself into a vault nobody has actually cleared. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Isolate and blank the line | Carry and place | A valve that is merely shut is still a valve — line pressure, a seat that has not fully seated, or somebody three streets over opening it from a SCADA screen can all put water back through it while an entrant is standing in the vault. The blanking plate is a solid steel disc bolted straight across the flange gap; it is the one form of isolation on this job that a hand at a keyboard somewhere else cannot undo. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Lock the isolation | Select | A padlock through the chain does something a closed valve on its own does not: it puts the isolation in the name of a specific person rather than a shift, so nobody working the panel that afternoon can wonder whether it is safe to operate. It stays on for as long as anyone could be below, and the only hand that ever takes it off again is the one that put it there. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Start mechanical ventilation | Select | The blower has to be moving clean air before anyone treats this vault as breathable, and where its intake sits decides whether that is even true — an intake set over standing water or downwind of an idling truck draws the exact hazard it exists to dilute straight down the duct. It runs from before the first reading is taken until after the last boot is back on the footway, because a shaft like this one does not stay ventilated on its own. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Test the atmosphere in order | Sequence (strict order: oxygen, flammable gas, toxic gas) | Oxygen goes first because a combustible-gas reading is only meaningful in a normal oxygen atmosphere — read for flammables first in an oxygen-deficient vault and the meter can hand back a false all-clear. Sampling top, middle and bottom in that order also catches a layered atmosphere that a single reading taken at the hatch would miss completely, since the heavier gases this vault can hold settle toward the bottom long before they ever reach the rim. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Confirm the oxygen reading | Graded reading | 19.5 to 23.5 percent is the whole of the acceptable range, and it is narrow because both directions fail differently — drop below it and a person can black out mid-sentence with nothing beforehand to tip them off, climb above it and ordinary things like a cotton sleeve or a smear of grease turn far more willing to burn than they look. That reading has to hold steady in the band before anyone treats the vault as entered, not just glanced at once from the hatch. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Rig the retrieval system | Select | A vertical entry like this one needs the tripod standing and the winch line run out before anyone clips a harness to it, because the alternative is a rescue that starts with somebody topside hunting through a truck for equipment while the clock that actually matters — the one on an entrant who has stopped answering — keeps running regardless. Rigged first, the retrieval system is already doing its job the instant it is needed instead of an unmeasured number of minutes after. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Fit the full-body harness | Select | The dorsal D-ring sits between the shoulder blades because that is the one attachment point that lets a winch draw somebody upright through an opening barely wider than their shoulders, rather than folding them double or dragging them face-first up the shaft wall. Clip the line anywhere else on the harness and a non-entry rescue turns into something the attendant has to improvise on the spot. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Establish continuous communication | Timed hold | The attendant's entire job reduces to two rules — stay in contact, and never go in yourself — and continuous genuinely means continuous, not a check-in every couple of minutes. This vault holds standing water at the bottom and a sewer tie-in that breathes with the mains, either of which can turn the air bad between one reading and the next, and the entrant going quiet on the radio is the only warning anyone topside gets before that becomes an emergency instead of a job. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Close the permit | Select | A permit does not close itself the moment the last boot clears the ladder — it closes against a headcount, with the space secured and the isolation still standing until the supervisor is satisfied nobody is unaccounted for. A permit left open while the crew is already coiling hose is exactly the condition that gets somebody sent back down alone, on nobody's authority, to fetch a dropped tool. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `rescue-entry` | You climbed down after the entrant. NIOSH's own tally of confined-space fatalities keeps landing on the same finding: the majority of the bodies recovered are not the worker the crew came to save, they are the coworker who followed without a plan, a line, or air of their own. The attendant's job right now is to raise the alarm and let the tripod and winch do the pulling, not to add a second casualty to the bottom of the shaft. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `open-hatch-unattended` | You left the opening unguarded. An open vault in a footway takes a pedestrian straight down before anyone can shout. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `petrol-blower` | That is a petrol blower sitting at the opening. Running an engine at the intake pumps carbon monoxide straight into the space you are about to breathe. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `no-blank` | The valve is only closed, not blanked. A closed valve is not an isolation — it can be operated remotely or leak past while somebody is inside the line. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Abatement Chamber (SmartCiti.X · `abatement-chamber`)

**Category:** Water & Environmental  
**Trade:** Asbestos / lead abatement worker  
**Certification / standard claimed:** LIUNA abatement workers; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1101, the asbestos standard for construction, and 29 CFR 1910.134 respiratory protection; EPA AHERA worker accreditation and the EPA asbestos NESHAP for the waste; the project design and clearance criteria in the containment plan  
**Tagline:** Containment integrity, wet-method removal and the three-stage decon airlock  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the containment work plan | Select | The plan is what sets the containment class, the respirator, the waste route and the clearance criteria for this specific material, and friable pipe insulation is a different job from intact lead paint on a handrail even though the poly looks the same. It also states the negative pressure this enclosure has to hold, which is the number you will be committing to on the manometer in a few minutes. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Walk the critical barriers | Find (any order: the lifted seam on the barrier, the tear at the floor-to-wall joint, the supply diffuser nobody sealed) | The poly is the only thing between this work and the rest of an occupied building, and it fails at seams, at the floor line and at the openings somebody forgot rather than in the middle of a sheet. You find those with your eyes and a hand on the plastic before the machine runs, because after that the enclosure is under pressure and every gap is a measured leak you are pulling building air through. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Start the negative-air machine | Select | The machine is what actually makes the enclosure negative, and it runs continuously for the whole job — through breaks, through lunch, through the night if the job runs over — not only while somebody happens to be inside. The filter is HEPA because anything coarser simply relocates the fibre, and the duct discharges outdoors because an exhaust dumped into a corridor has abated nothing. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Confirm negative pressure on the manometer | Graded reading | Negative pressure is what makes air fall into the enclosure every time the flap opens instead of blowing out of it, and it is a number on a manometer rather than an impression from the machine sounding busy. A unit can run flat out against a containment so leaky it never develops any pressure at all, and the gauge is the only thing that tells those two situations apart. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Don PPE in the correct order | Sequence (strict order: coveralls, respirator, taped gloves and boot covers) | The respirator seals against skin, so it goes on after the suit but before the hood — pull the hood up first and you have a facepiece sealing against a sheet of polypropylene, which is not a seal at all. The tape goes on last because it is what stops a sleeve riding up when you reach overhead, and reaching overhead is the whole of this job. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Hold the user seal check | Timed hold | A negative-pressure seal check is held, not flicked at: you block the inlets, breathe in, and the facepiece has to stay drawn against your face for the whole count without creeping back out. That is the difference between a respirator and a piece of rubber near your face, and OSHA's respiratory protection standard asks for it every single time the mask goes on — not once a year at the fit test. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Wet the material with amended water | Tracked hold | Amended water carries a surfactant so it wets through the material rather than beading on it, and that only happens if it is put on gently. Hit friable insulation with a hard jet and you aerosolise exactly the fibre you were trying to bind, inside a containment, at head height. Too light and you have only damped the face, so the first thing your scraper reaches is still dry. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Remove the wetted material | Select | A section small enough to stay wet through the whole of its removal is the only size worth starting, because insulation dries from the moment you open it and a big run outruns the sprayer. Material that dries in your hands is dry removal, whatever the plan says, and the enclosure is now holding airborne fibre instead of the damp lumps it was designed around. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Double-bag the waste and take it to the load-out | Carry and place | Two bags, because the outer one is what stays clean enough to leave the enclosure, and a label because everybody downstream — the hauler, the scale house, the landfill operator, an inspector years later — has a right to know what they are handling. It leaves through the load-out rather than the decon airlock so that waste and people never use the same opening. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Exit through the three-stage decon | Sequence (strict order: dirty room, shower, clean room) | Each stage takes off one layer and there is no other way out of this enclosure. Suit and boot covers come off in the dirty room, the shower takes what is on your skin and hair with the respirator still on your face, and only the clean room holds your own clothes. Go through it backwards and you have carried the whole shift's contamination into the one room that was clean. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Remove the respirator in the clean room | Select | The outside of that facepiece is the dirtiest surface you own, and the shower ran with it on for exactly that reason. This is the first point on the way out where the air around your face has been through the decon too, so it is the first point where taking the mask off does not simply undo the last ten minutes. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Close out the containment log | Select | The log is the evidence that this enclosure actually held the pressure the plan called for, for the hours it was occupied, and that every bag is accounted for on the manifest. It is also where the clearance sampling goes, because the containment does not come down on somebody's opinion that the area looks clean — it comes down on a result, and the inspector reads that first. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `containment-flap` | You pushed through the containment flap without confirming negative pressure on the manometer. If the enclosure isn't actually under negative pressure, opening it pushes fibres out into the building instead of holding them in. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `dry-removal-tool` | That is a dry scraper. Working the material dry aerosolises fibres immediately — the entire point of the wet method is that a wetted material does not go airborne when it is disturbed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `early-respirator-removal` | You reached to pull the respirator off before finishing the decon shower. Contamination sits on the outside of that mask and on your skin and hair — it comes off only once you are standing in the clean room. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `unlabeled-bag` | That waste bag is neither double-bagged nor labeled, and it is sitting in the clean side of the airlock. An unlabeled asbestos or lead bag in a clean area is exactly how contamination leaves the site undetected. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `break-mug` | That is somebody's coffee, inside the regulated area. Eating, drinking and smoking in a regulated area are prohibited outright by the asbestos standard, for the obvious reason: the respirator has to come off to do any of them, and fibre that settled on the rim of that mug goes straight down somebody's throat. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Lift Station (SmartCiti.X · `lift-station`)

**Category:** Water & Environmental  
**Trade:** Wastewater collection system operator  
**Certification / standard claimed:** AFSCME / LIUNA — state wastewater collection system operator certification (CWEA Collection System Maintenance Grade II or equivalent); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 permit-required confined space; 1910.147 lockout/tagout  
**Tagline:** Wet-well pump pull: gas test, lockout, bypass pumping, guide-rail lift, no-entry retrieval, restart and level check  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the work order and the well data | Select | The order names the pump that tripped and the plan names how the flow keeps moving while it is out on the pad. A crew that starts pulling before the bypass plan is set is scheduling an overflow, not preventing one — the catchment above this station does not pause for maintenance. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Test the wet-well atmosphere through the vent | Sequence (strict order: oxygen, flammable gas, hydrogen sulfide) | Testing through the vent with the hatch still closed means the first reading is taken with nobody's face anywhere near the opening it turns out to be bad news at. Oxygen is read first because the flammable sensor's catalytic bead cannot be trusted at all in an oxygen-deficient atmosphere, which a sewer headspace routinely is. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Lock out the duty pump | Turn | The level controller does not know a pump is on the chain — it will call for the duty pump the instant the well rises past its set point, exactly as it does on any ordinary night. Your lock is the only thing standing between that call and a four-hundred-kilogram pump trying to start while it hangs in the shaft. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Set up bypass pumping | Sequence (strict order: suction hose in the well, discharge to the downstream manhole, bypass pump start) | Suction and discharge are both connected before the pump ever starts, because starting it with the discharge still open is not a delay, it is a spill onto the ground next to the crew. The bypass exists to take the inflow the duty pump was carrying so the well can be worked on without the level climbing behind everyone's back. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Confirm the bypass is holding the level | Graded reading | A bypass that cannot hold the level down is not a bypass, it is a smaller pump adding a false sense of coverage to the same problem. The level has to sit demonstrably below the set point before anyone commits to pulling the duty pump, because once that pump is on the chain there is nothing else in the well to catch a rise. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Open the hatch and set the guard | Select | The hatch opens onto a four-metre drop into a permit space with hydrogen sulfide sitting in the bottom of it. The grate is what keeps a foot, a tool or a person on the surface once that opening exists, while the pump itself is what actually comes up through it on the rail. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Lift the pump on the guide rail | Timed hold | The pump breaks its mechanical seal off the discharge elbow at the bottom of the rail and then rides that rail all the way to the top, guided the whole way so it never swings free over the shaft. A stalled lift leaves four hundred kilograms hanging half out of a permit space on a chain, which is its own hazard on top of the one already down there. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Land the pump on the pad | Carry and place | The pump gets handled on solid ground, never in the air, because a load on a chain can shift the instant a hand touches it and a hoist is not a hand rated to catch anything. Hands go on the pump only after the chain has gone slack and the weight is fully on the pad, not before. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Find the fault on the pad | Find (any order: ragged impeller) | The whole pull exists to find whatever tripped this pump, and it gets found here, on the pad, in daylight, with the pump locked out and sitting flat on the ground — never on the chain, and never by reaching into the wet well to check it in place, which is exactly the shortcut this pull was designed to avoid. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Rail the pump back, close the hatch, remove the lock, restart | Select | Everything goes back in reverse order for a reason: the well is closed before the bypass comes off so nothing is exposed while flow transfers back, and the lock comes off last, by the same person who put it on, because that lock was never anyone else's to remove. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `well-ladder` | You started down the wet-well ladder. This is a permit-required confined space with hydrogen sulfide in it; the pump comes out on the guide rail from the top, and nobody goes down without a permit, an attendant and retrieval — which is not this job. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `hatch-no-gas` | You opened the hatch before the gas test. The first breath at the opening is the one the meter is for — H2S at the concentration a wet well can hold takes a person down at the hatch, not at the bottom. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `run-no-bypass` | You pulled the duty pump with no bypass running. The inflow does not stop for maintenance; without bypass pumping, the well overflows into the street and the neighbourhood's basements inside the hour. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Chlorine Room (SmartCiti.X · `chlorine-room`)

**Category:** Water & Environmental  
**Trade:** Water treatment plant operator  
**Certification / standard claimed:** State / AWWA Water Treatment Operator Grade II; Chlorine Institute Pamphlets 1 and 65 (cylinder handling, Emergency Kit A); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1000 chlorine PEL and 1910.134 respiratory protection; NFPA 55 compressed gas storage  
**Tagline:** 150-lb chlorine cylinder change: room monitor and SCBA before the door, empty isolated and capped, full one on the scale and chained, new gasket, yoke a quarter turn past snug, ammonia leak test, valve one turn, wrench on the stem  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the SOP and today's feed rate | Select | The SOP names the setpoint the plant needs and the two-person rule for the room, and it exists because a chlorine cylinder change is not a job to improvise under time pressure — every line in it removes one way to end up standing in a room with a rising concentration and no plan already agreed to. The change is done the same way every time so the one time it leaks, the response is a habit already rehearsed, not a decision made from scratch with an alarm already sounding. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Check the room monitor | Graded reading | The monitor is the only thing that smells chlorine before you do at a concentration that matters — the OSHA PEL sits well below the level a human nose reliably notices, so by the time you can smell it yourself the room may already be past the ceiling limit. It is read and bump-tested before the door opens every time, because a sensor that has drifted or died is worse than no sensor at all: it tells you the room is clear when it no longer has any way of knowing. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Stage the SCBA and post the outside operator | Sequence (any order: SCBA at the door, outside operator) | Nobody works a chlorine cylinder alone in this room. The pack is staged at the door because the leak, if it comes, comes at the yoke where you are standing — Chlorine Institute Pamphlet 65's Emergency Kit A assumes a response starts within seconds of a release, not minutes, and an SCBA fetched from a locker down the hall after the alarm sounds is a rescue that has already lost the only window that mattered. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Close the empty cylinder's valve | Turn | The regulator comes off a closed valve, never an open one — cracking a fitting on a cylinder still under pressure sprays chlorine gas straight at whoever's hands are on the wrench. The cylinder reads 'empty' at roughly 20 lb residual, not zero, and that residual is still under enough vapour pressure to empty itself through any fitting left open, which is exactly why the valve is proven fully closed before anything downstream of it is touched. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Remove the regulator, cap and hood the empty | Sequence (strict order: vacuum regulator, outlet cap, valve hood) | The cap seals the outlet and the hood protects the valve stem for the trip across the room and the ride back to the supplier — Chlorine Institute Pamphlet 1 treats an uncapped valve as the single failure that turns a dropped or rolled cylinder into a full release, because a snapped valve stem on a cylinder this size empties the entire remaining charge in well under a minute with nothing left to shut it off. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Bring the full cylinder onto the scale | Carry and place | The scale is how the plant knows what is actually left in service rather than trusting a gauge or a guess: feed is confirmed by weight loss over the shift, and a cylinder is called empty at roughly 20 lb residual rather than run to zero, because a cylinder emptied of usable chlorine still holds a vapour pressure that will happily push whatever residual remains straight out through any fitting left open. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Chain the cylinder and fit a new gasket | Sequence (any order: restraint chain, new lead gasket) | A chained cylinder cannot fall on its own valve, and a 150-lb cylinder falling on an unprotected valve stem is exactly the impact that snaps one off. A new lead gasket at every connection is the Chlorine Institute's own rule rather than a convenience, because a lead gasket seals by taking a single controlled crush — reusing one that has already taken that crush leaves a joint that looks tight and weeps chlorine the moment pressure comes up behind it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Tighten the yoke | Graded reading | The lead gasket seals by taking a controlled crush, and a quarter turn past hand-tight is the amount of crush that seals the joint without going further: less than that and the gasket never fully seats, so it weeps chlorine at the yoke as soon as pressure comes on; more than that crushes the gasket into the valve threads and leaves a damaged sealing face that the next change inherits whether or not the gasket itself gets replaced. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Ammonia leak test every joint | Timed hold | Ammonia vapour meets chlorine gas and makes a visible white ammonium chloride cloud at a concentration of only a few parts per million, well below what most people can smell and far below anything an eye could catch on a bare joint — which is why every yoke, every regulator fitting and every valve packing gets tested with the bottle before the cylinder goes into service, not just the ones that look suspect. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Open the valve one turn | Turn | One full turn of a chlorine cylinder valve gives full flow through the regulator; turning it further only adds turns that have to be found again by feel if the valve needs shutting fast in a leak. The wrench stays seated on the stem for exactly that reason — the first motion in an emergency has to be closing the valve, and a wrench that has to be located first is seconds a chlorine release in an enclosed room does not give back. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Set the feed rate | Graded reading | The setpoint is the chlorine residual the plant is required to hold at the customer's tap, not a number set to look busy on the rotameter: too little and pathogens the disinfection step exists to kill can survive the required contact time, too much and the plant fields taste-and-odour complaints while paying to feed chlorine that leaves through the vent as unused excess residual. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Walk the room before leaving | Find (any order: wrench off the stem) | The room is left the way the next leak — not this shift's leak, whichever one comes next — actually needs it: the wrench seated on the in-service valve stem where an emergency response starts, Kit A sealed and within reach rather than checked once a quarter, the door closed, and the monitor confirmed live rather than assumed live because it was live yesterday. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `no-scba-entry` | You went into the chlorine room with no SCBA staged and nobody outside. A leak in there is one breath from a hospital; the air pack at the door and the operator watching through the window are what turn a leak into a procedure instead of a rescue. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `reused-gasket` | You reused the old lead gasket. A lead gasket crushes once to seal; the second time it seals until the pressure comes on and then weeps chlorine at the yoke all night. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `water-on-leak` | You put water on a chlorine leak. Chlorine and water make hydrochloric acid — the leak corrodes wider, the cloud grows, and the room becomes an entry for a hazmat team. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `roll-uncapped` | You moved a cylinder with the valve uncapped and unhooded. A snapped valve on a 150-lb cylinder empties it into the room in minutes; the cap and hood go on before the cylinder moves an inch. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
