## Fire Pump (SmartCiti.X · `fire-pump`)

**Category:** Building Systems & Facilities  
**Trade:** Fire sprinkler fitter / fire pump technician  
**Certification / standard claimed:** UA — journeyman sprinkler fitter; NFPA 25 (inspection, testing and maintenance of water-based systems) annual fire pump flow test; NICET Inspection & Testing of Water-Based Systems  
**Tagline:** Annual pump flow test: alarm notification, controller to manual, test header to safe discharge, churn / 100% / 150% points, curve compared, system restored  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the test record and the nameplate curve | Select | The nameplate states what the pump is rated to deliver — flow, pressure, rpm — and last year's NFPA 25 test record states what it actually delivered a year ago. This year's churn, 100% and 150% readings are judged against both curves, because a pump that still meets its nameplate but has drifted from last year's numbers is already telling you something is wearing. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Notify the alarm company and the building | Select | Running the pump sends a pump-running signal to the monitoring company exactly the way a real fire would, and an un-notified signal gets a fire department dispatched to a building with nothing burning. Putting the account on test before the pump turns holds that dispatch for the window, and calling back afterward takes the building off test before the next real signal needs to be believed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Confirm suction and the supply valve open | Graded reading | A centrifugal fire pump needs a positive column of water at its suction before it is ever called to run; a closed control valve or a dropped municipal supply starves the impeller of the water it needs to cool and lubricate itself. That shows up on this gauge first — read before the pump is started, not after the bearings have already cooked. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Lay the test hoses to a safe discharge | Sequence (strict order: hose lines from the test header, discharge to the outside, playpipe nozzles with pitot access) | The test flows the pump's full rated capacity — a thousand gallons a minute or more — and where that water goes has to be decided before the header valve opens, not while it is running. Lines laid outside to a discharge that can actually take it, playpipes secured so the pitot readings hold steady, keep that flow from finding the nearest person or the pump room floor instead. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Controller to manual test | Turn | In manual, the pump starts and stops on your command alone. Left in automatic during the test, a pressure drop anywhere on the system — even one your own hoses cause — starts the pump before you are positioned to read it, and the controller's own timer can stop it again mid-reading and void the point. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Start the pump at churn | Select | Churn — the no-flow point — is the first reading on the curve, and it also proves the motor starts, comes up to rated speed and holds steady discharge pressure before a gallon of water moves. A large fire-pump motor coming up to speed is loud enough to trigger OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.95 hearing-conservation threshold, so hearing protection goes on with the start command, not after the noise surprises you. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Read the churn pressure | Graded reading | Churn pressure sitting above the nameplate band means the relief valve is holding it there correctly; well below it points to a worn impeller, a slipping coupling or the pump running at the wrong speed. It is the first number written on the test sheet, and every reading after it is judged against this one. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Open the header to 100% flow | Graded reading | Rated flow at rated pressure is the exact point stamped on the pump's nameplate, and hitting it is the one reading that says this pump can still deliver what the building's sprinkler design assumed it could. Miss it low and every sprinkler head downstream of this pump is protected by less water than the design called for. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Hold the 150% flow point | Timed hold | At 150% of rated flow, NFPA 25 requires the pump still make at least 65% of its rated pressure — the point where a worn impeller or a slipping motor shows up hardest. Current, speed and pressure are all read with the flow held steady at that point, not caught on the way past it while the needle is still moving. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Read current and speed | Sequence (any order: motor current, pump speed) | Pressure alone can hide a motor slipping under load or a pump running slower than its rated speed while still making a pressure that looks acceptable on the gauge. Motor current on each phase and pump rpm from the tachometer are what tie that pressure back to the curve and catch a fault the discharge gauge alone would miss. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Close the header, controller to automatic, call the alarm company back | Select | A fire pump left in manual mode will not start itself for a real fire — it will sit at the panel waiting for a hand that is not there. Closing the header, confirming the supply valve open, returning the selector to automatic and calling the alarm company off test is the last sequence of the job, and the one that actually returns the building's protection. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Walk the pump room before locking up | Find (any order: packing gland running dry) | Running the pump at full flow heats bearings, stresses the packing and shakes loose whatever the room was hiding while it sat idle for a year. The walk-through right after, while everything is still warm and still moving, is where a gland running dry gets caught and adjusted, not left to score a shaft sleeve before next year's test finds it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `no-notify-run` | You started the pump without notifying the alarm company. A fire pump running trips the waterflow and pump-running signals — the fire department rolls to a building with no fire, and the next real signal from this building gets a slower response. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `flow-indoors` | You opened the test header with the discharge pointed into the pump room. Two thousand gallons a minute at 100 psi fills the room, floods the controller and knocks a person off their feet; the hose lines go to the outside discharge. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `suction-closed` | You started the pump with the suction control valve closed. A centrifugal pump with no water at the suction cavitates and destroys its impeller and seal in minutes — the suction gauge is read before the pump is called. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `bypass-controller` | You jumpered the controller to force the pump on. The controller is the listed device that starts, runs and protects the pump; jumpered, it has no overload, no phase protection and no record of the run. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Cooling Tower (SmartCiti.X · `cooling-tower`)

**Category:** Building Systems & Facilities  
**Trade:** Stationary engineer — water treatment and cooling towers  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IUOE Local stationary engineer; ASHRAE 188 building water management program and Guideline 12 Legionella control; CDC / OSHA Legionella toolkit for cooling towers; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 respiratory protection and 1910.147 lockout/tagout; EPA FIFRA-registered biocide label compliance  
**Tagline:** Quarterly clean and Legionella control: plan and last culture read, tower down and fan locked, respirator before the basin, biofilm physically removed, drift eliminator checked, biocide shock to the label, conductivity and halogen back in range, log signed  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the water management plan | Select | ASHRAE 188 makes this plan the single document the building is judged against, by a health department or by an outbreak investigator, whichever comes first. Every control limit, every dose calculation and every entry in today's log traces back to a number written on this board, not to what worked on a previous tower or what feels safe by habit. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Read the last culture | Select | A rising culture count changes what this visit actually is: a routine clean and a disinfection are different tasks with different dose rates and different documentation, and the number on this report decides which one you are doing today. It also decides whether the building's risk group — the people most likely to get sick from an aerosol release — has to be notified before the basin is even opened. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Shut down and lock out the fan | Sequence (strict order: tower off at the panel, fan breaker open, lock and tag) | Taking the tower off at the control panel only silences the automation's normal call to run — it does not stop a scheduled restart, an override, or somebody two floors down who has no idea you are up here. A fan that turns over while you are in the basin is both a direct mechanical hazard and an aerosol release over the roof and the intake below it. The lock on the breaker is the one thing here that makes the shutdown physically impossible to undo rather than just administratively likely. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Put on respiratory and chemical protection | Sequence (any order: half-face respirator with P100, coveralls and chemical gloves, eyewash station checked) | This task carries two separate exposures that need different protection: the aerosol coming off a disturbed basin, which the P100 respirator is rated to filter, and the concentrated biocide handled at full strength before it is diluted into the tower, which the chemical gloves and a working eyewash station exist for. Skipping either one leaves exactly one of those exposures completely uncovered. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Drain the basin | Turn | The basin drains to the sanitary connection and never to storm, because what comes out of it is treated water carrying a biocide residual and whatever biological load has been growing in the system — exactly the kind of discharge storm drains are built to carry straight into a waterway untreated. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Wet-wash the basin and fill | Timed hold | The clean has to be physical, not chemical: biofilm is a structure the organism builds specifically to protect itself, and a biocide poured over an intact layer never reaches what is living underneath it. Low pressure and wet surfaces keep whatever comes off from turning into the exact airborne dust this entire procedure exists to prevent. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Inspect the drift eliminator and sump | Find (any order: gap in the drift eliminator, debris in the sump screen) | The drift eliminator is arguably the single most important piece of Legionella control hardware on this whole tower, because it is the one component whose entire job is stopping aerosol from leaving the unit at all. Every dose, every control limit and every culture result in the plan assumes that barrier is intact — a gap in it lets untreated droplets past all of that chemistry and out over the roof. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Dose the biocide shock | Graded reading | The label rate is calculated specifically against this basin's own volume, and under FIFRA it is not a guideline, it is enforceable law. Dose under it and the shock does close to nothing to the biofilm you just cleaned off; dose over it and the excess goes out with the discharge as a permit violation while also accelerating corrosion on every metal surface the water touches. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Hold the contact time | Tracked hold | Microbial kill is concentration multiplied by time, not concentration alone — a strong dose held for half the required period does roughly the same nothing as a weak dose held for the full one. Letting the residual drop mid-contact hands the advantage straight back to whatever organism survived in the biofilm just scraped off, and it recolonises from there. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Test free halogen | Graded reading | The tower returns to service running at the operating residual, not at the shock concentration just used to kill the biofilm — those are two different numbers doing two different jobs. The operating band is what the plan's control limit is actually written against, and it is the number that goes in the log for the next inspection to check the tower against. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Return to service and sign the log | Sequence (strict order: lock removed, tower back in service, log signed and next culture booked) | The signed log is both the building's institutional memory and its defence: it is the record that this exact service happened, on this date, to this specification. The first time a health department or an outbreak investigator asks for it, an unsigned entry reads exactly like a service that was never performed at all, regardless of what actually happened up here. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `fan-live-basin` | You opened the basin with the fan running. A disturbed basin aerosolises everything in it, and the fan puts that plume over the roof, the intake and the street — this is exactly how a building outbreak starts. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `dry-brush-biofilm` | You dry-brushed the biofilm. Dry scale and biofilm go airborne as respirable dust carrying the organism; the surfaces are kept wet through the whole clean for that reason. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `no-respirator` | You went into the basin with no respiratory protection. A cooling tower basin at cleaning is the highest-exposure task in the building, and a surgical mask is not respiratory protection. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `dose-off-label` | You dosed the biocide off the label rate. The label is enforceable law under FIFRA: under-dose and the shock does nothing to the biofilm, over-dose and the discharge is a permit violation and a corrosion event. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Vapor Mitigation (SmartCiti.X · `vapor-mitigation`)

**Category:** Building Systems & Facilities  
**Trade:** Sub-slab depressurisation system installer  
**Certification / standard claimed:** UA Local 38 plumbers and pipefitters on the piping and vessel work; IBEW Local 6 electricians on the fan circuit under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 control of hazardous energy; LIUNA hazmat laborers on cuttings and waste handling; system design and commissioning per ASTM E2121 sub-slab depressurisation practice, the EPA OSWER vapor intrusion technical guide, and California DTSC's vapor intrusion guidance  
**Tagline:** Commissioning a sub-slab depressurisation system: communication proven at every test point, the fan circuit proven dead before the housing opens, the fan hung and vented clear of any intake, the vacuum verified against design, and an indoor-air sample sealed under chain of custody  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the mitigation design | Select | The print is what says how many test points prove this system, what vacuum counts as holding at each one, and where the discharge is allowed to terminate. None of that is decided on site by feel — it was sized to the plume and the slab this building actually sits on. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Walk the room before the system goes live | Find (any order: unsealed slab penetration, open floor-drain sump lid) | Every uncontrolled opening in this floor is a path the vacuum field will take instead of the path the design intended. Finding them now, before the fan ever runs, is the difference between commissioning a system and troubleshooting one that never worked. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Run the sub-slab communication test | Tracked hold | This is the whole premise of the system proven before the fan is ever installed: that the sub-slab is one pneumatically connected space, so that one fan pulling on one pit actually reaches every test point on the print. A system installed on a slab that never passed this test is a fan pulling on a pocket of gravel, not the plume underneath the building. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Prove the fan circuit dead before the housing opens | Sequence (strict order: fan circuit breaker opened, lock and tag applied, circuit tested dead) | Open, then lock and tag, then test: that order is 1910.147 itself. A breaker left merely open can be closed by anyone who does not see a tag on it, and a circuit that has never actually been tested is only assumed dead — the fan's own terminal block is the last thing to trust that assumption on. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Hang the fan on its hangers | Carry and place | The fan hangs on its own strap hangers, isolated from the riser it connects to, so the piping is never carrying the fan's weight or its vibration. A fan resting on the pipe instead of its hangers eventually cracks the very joint it depends on to pull a vacuum. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Make up the riser coupling | Turn | This joint is what carries the entire vacuum the fan generates down to the pit and the gravel beneath it. Made up to the design's mark by hand it seals; short of it, it leaks air the fan then wastes its whole capacity drawing through instead of through the slab. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Land the fan's leads and close the housing | Sequence (strict order: ground landed, neutral landed, hot landed, housing closed and latched) | Ground first and hot last is the whole point of the order: a ground that is already landed protects everyone working the rest of the box, and the hot conductor is the one you want in your hand for the shortest time possible, connected last with the circuit already proven dead. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Restore the fan circuit | Select | Power comes back only once the housing is closed — a fan proven dead for the wiring stays proven dead until there is nothing left inside it for a hand to reach, which is exactly what a closed and latched housing means. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Route the discharge above the eave | Carry and place | Everything this fan pulls out of the sub-slab has to go somewhere that is not back into this building or the one beside it. Terminated above the eave and clear of any intake, it disperses; terminated low or near a louvre, the system spends its whole life feeding the exact vapor intrusion it exists to stop back through the nearest open window. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Set the system manometer | Graded reading | The manometer is the system's own permanent readout — the thing a building engineer glances at every day long after this crew has left. Set correctly now, a falling reading months from now is the first and only warning that the system has stopped protecting the building. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Set the alarm set point | Turn | The alarm is what tells a building engineer the fan has failed on a Tuesday afternoon rather than the system quietly doing nothing until the next annual inspection finds it. Set below the proven operating point, it trips on an actual loss of vacuum instead of on the system's own normal fluctuation. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Verify vacuum at every test point | Graded reading | The communication test proved the slab is one connected space; this is the proof the running system actually holds the design's minimum vacuum at the point furthest from the pit, which is the point that fails first if anything is wrong. A system that holds at the pit and fails at the far corner is a system that has not been verified at all. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Take the indoor-air sample | Timed hold | This canister is what actually answers the question the whole job exists to answer: is the air in this building, right now, with the system running, safe to breathe. Every other reading in this station is a proxy for this one. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Label and seal the sample's chain of custody | Sequence (strict order: canister labelled with location, date and time, custody seal applied) | An unlabelled or unsealed canister is a result nobody downstream can trust to be this room, on this day, under this system's operation — and a mitigation system's whole case rests on a sample the lab and the regulator both believe. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 15 | Sign the operations and maintenance placard | Select | This placard is the only part of the whole job that stays in the room after the crew leaves. A building engineer who finds the alarm tripped six months from now acts on what this placard says, not on what anyone remembers about today. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `housing-live` | You reached into the fan's terminal housing before its circuit was proven dead. OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.147 exists exactly for this moment: a fan motor's terminal block carries line voltage until somebody has actually locked the breaker, tagged it and tested it dead, and 'it's probably off' is not a control — it is a guess made with a hand inside an energised enclosure. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `tape-not-seal` | You reached for the tape to close the slab crack instead of a proper mechanical or urethane seal. A sub-slab depressurisation system only works if the vacuum field it pulls stays under the slab; a taped crack peels the first time the slab flexes with the season, and the system starts pulling conditioned building air instead of soil vapor without ever telling anyone it failed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `wrench-riser` | You reached for the pipe wrench on a solvent-welded PVC riser. This joint is sized and torqued by the design, by hand, not by however hard a wrench can turn it — over-torquing a schedule-40 PVC coupling cracks the fitting, and a crack in a vacuum riser never shows itself until the fan is straining to hold a field it cannot reach. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `discharge-near-intake` | You routed the discharge toward the low vent instead of above the eave. ASTM E2121 and the EPA's vapor intrusion guidance both require the fan discharge clear of any door, window or air intake specifically so the vapor it just pulled out of the sub-slab does not walk straight back into the building — or the one next door — on the next gust. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Cath Lab (SmartCiti.X · `cath-lab`)

**Category:** Building Systems & Facilities  
**Trade:** Hospital facilities electrician / health care building engineer  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IBEW and IUOE hospital locals — health care facility maintenance; NFPA 99 health care facilities code for patient care space categories and the essential electrical system; NFPA 70 Article 517 for health care facility wiring, isolated power systems and the reference grounding point; NFPA 70E for the risk assessment at the panel; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 control of hazardous energy; the hospital's own interim life safety measures and its written clinical authorisation to take the room down  
**Tagline:** Planned outage on a cath lab branch panel: clinical authorisation and a window with nobody on the table, the life-safety branch left alone, isolated power read rather than silenced, grounding tested rather than assumed, room confirmed by the clinical team before hand-back  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Take the written clinical authorisation | Select | This is the document that turns a work order into permission. It names the room, the branch, the agreed start and the agreed return, and it carries the signature of somebody clinical who is accountable for there being nobody on the table when it starts. Without it you have a maintenance system telling you a date, which is a plan, and plans in a procedure suite lose to whatever came through the door at four in the morning. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Find the three branches and the one that is yours | Find (any order: life safety branch, critical branch, equipment branch) | An essential electrical system is not one supply with a label on it. Life safety, critical and equipment are wired, fed and transferred separately so that losing one cannot take the others, and in a plant room they sit side by side in near-identical enclosures with the schedules behind the doors. Reading all three and saying out loud which one is on the permit is the last cheap moment in this job; everything after it costs a room. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Get the room released at the board | Select | The authorisation says the room can be released; only the person running the list can say it is released now. The question is answered off the day's board and out loud: nobody on the table, nothing queued into this room, and the on-call room identified in case a case arrives while you are inside the panel. It is also how the clinical team learn who you are and where you will be, which is what makes the next hour's interruptions land on the right person. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Put the interim life safety measures in | Sequence (strict order: impairment logged, alarm desk and clinical engineering told, room signed out of service) | Taking part of a hospital's systems out of service starts a clock that somebody else is responsible for, so it is logged rather than mentioned. The alarm desk needs to know which devices in this room will be silent and for how long, clinical engineering needs to know their equipment is about to lose its supply rather than fail, and the sign on the door is what stops the room being used by a team who had no way of knowing. All three before the breaker, because after it they are explanations rather than measures. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Read the line isolation monitor before you start | Graded reading | The monitor is continuously measuring how much current would flow if a first fault to ground appeared anywhere on this isolated system, and that figure rises quietly as every long cord, every damp connection and every extra piece of equipment in the room adds its own leakage. Reading it now gives you the baseline you will compare against afterwards. Skip it and any alarm later in the shift is unattributable — you will not be able to say whether your work caused it or found it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Open the equipment branch breaker | Turn | The one on the permit, in the panelboard you identified, verified against the schedule on the door and against the circuit you are about to work — three separate confirmations for one handle, because the two panelboards either side of it feed things that must not go off. Taken fully to off rather than tripped part way, so there is no argument later about whether the mechanism actually opened or merely moved. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Lock and tag it in your own name | Select | A hospital's electrical distribution is watched by a building management system, switched by automatic transfer and attended by people whose entire job is to put supplies back on when they notice one missing. None of them know your hands are inside an outlet box. Your own lock with your own name on it is the only device in the building that outranks the instinct to restore a supply, and the name matters because it tells the person who finds it who to phone instead of cutting it off. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Prove the circuit dead — and prove the meter | Graded reading | The test is only worth what the instrument is worth, and the way an instrument fails is by reading zero on everything. Proving unit, then circuit, then proving unit again catches the meter that died between the first reading and the second, which is the one failure mode that turns a careful electrician into a casualty. Every conductor, every combination, including the ones the schedule says are not there — an isolated system has no grounded conductor to reason from. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Hold the bond test on the reference grounding point | Timed hold | The reference grounding point is where every equipment grounding conductor in this patient care space is brought together, and the test asks whether the receptacle in your hand is genuinely connected to it. Held for the full count because the reading walks while the test current is establishing itself through whatever oxide and paint is in the path — and a short test reads whatever it happened to be doing while it was still deciding. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Read the equipment grounding path | Graded reading | The number means nothing on its own; it means something against the last one recorded for this room. A path that has drifted since the previous test has a termination going loose somewhere between the outlet box and the reference point, and finding it now — with the branch already locked out — costs an hour. Finding it later means opening the room again. Measure it, write it beside the previous figure, and let the two numbers argue. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Fit the hospital-grade receptacle | Carry and place | The green dot on the face is not decoration: a hospital-grade receptacle is built and tested for retention and for the integrity of its grounding contact, because in this room the thing plugged into it is attached to a patient and the cord gets dragged by a moving boom all day. A general-purpose device fitted here looks identical from a metre away, passes every functional test, and quietly removes the one property it was chosen for. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Prove the monitor by its own test function | Tracked hold | A line isolation monitor that no longer alarms is worse than none at all, because the room is being told it is protected by something that has stopped watching. Its own test function simulates the fault condition, and holding it steady is what lets you confirm that both the local indication and the remote annunciation actually operate — the lamp in this room and the point at the desk are two separate things, and only one of them is in front of you. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Put it back in order | Sequence (strict order: your lock off the hasp, equipment branch breaker closed, monitor back to its normal indication) | Your own lock comes off first, by you, because a lock removed by anybody else is the beginning of an investigation. The breaker closes next, and then the monitor is watched rather than glanced at: an isolated power system that has had work done on it will show you in the first few seconds whether what you did added leakage, and that indication is the only feedback the room gives you on your own work. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Hand the room back with the clinical team | Find (any order: monitor green, local and remote, the boom outlet proved under load, the clinical team's signature) | A hand-back is not an announcement, it is a demonstration. The monitor is shown green locally and at the desk, the receptacle is shown working under real load through the boom's full travel, and only then does somebody clinical sign for the room. Done this way the first case of the day is not the test, which is the whole difference between a maintenance department a suite trusts and one it schedules around. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `life-safety-breaker` | You opened a breaker in the life safety branch. It is in the same cupboard, on the same wall, in a panelboard that looks like the one you were sent to, and it feeds none of your work: it feeds the egress lighting, the exit signs, the fire alarm and the things that have to keep working precisely on the day everything else does not. The essential electrical system is divided into separate branches so that a fault or an outage on one of them cannot take the other two with it — and an electrician who opens the wrong one by hand has done in a second exactly what all that separation exists to prevent. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `no-clinical-ok` | You started on the strength of the schedule. A planned date in a maintenance system is a request, not a release: the only thing that can hand you a procedure room is the clinical team who are using it, on the day, when they have looked at the board and confirmed there is nobody on the table and no case queued behind. Rooms run late, cases get added, and a patient arrives in the one you have just locked out. The paperwork exists so that this is somebody's explicit decision rather than an assumption made by whoever turned up first. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `silence-lim` | You silenced the line isolation monitor. That alarm does not mean the isolated power system has failed and it does not mean the room has to stop — that is the whole design intent, and it is why silencing it feels harmless. What it means is that the total hazard current has climbed to where a first fault to ground is no longer the harmless event the system exists to make it, and the next fault will be a live path through whatever is between it and earth. The alarm is information about a condition you are supposed to go and find, and a silenced monitor is a room that has quietly stopped being an isolated power system. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `assume-ground` | You signed the grounding off the panel schedule. A schedule is a record of what somebody intended when the room was built and of every change they remembered to write down since. It is not a measurement. Equipment grounding conductors get lifted for a repair and left off, reference grounding point terminations get loosened by vibration, and a green wire landed on a screw that is no longer tight is indistinguishable from a good one until it is tested. In a room where the patient is connected to mains-powered equipment through catheters, the grounding is the protection, and protection is measured. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Ammonia Plant (SmartCiti.X · `ammonia-plant`)

**Category:** Building Systems & Facilities  
**Trade:** Industrial refrigeration operator / refrigeration fitter  
**Certification / standard claimed:** RETA CARO / CIRO industrial refrigeration operator; UA refrigeration service technicians and IUOE stationary engineers; IIAR 6 inspection, testing and maintenance and IIAR 2 machinery-room provisions; ASHRAE 15 refrigeration machinery rooms; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 process safety management where the charge is 10,000 lb or more; 1910.147 lockout/tagout; 1910.134 respiratory protection  
**Tagline:** Detection alarm on an arena ice plant: everything decided at the outside panel first, entry on air, circuit pumped down and locked, seal changed, discharge open before suction on the way back  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the alarm at the emergency control station | Select | The emergency control station is outside the machinery room on purpose, so every decision about the room is made by somebody who is not yet breathing what is in it. Which head and which set point is the difference between a seal weeping and a line letting go. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Start emergency ventilation from outside | Turn | The ventilation runs before the door opens, not after, so the room is already moving air to its own discharge by the time there is a gap in the wall. Started from outside because the switch you would have to walk in to reach is a switch you would have to walk into the release to reach. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Close the approach off | Carry and place | A machinery room with a live alarm has one person going towards it and everybody else going away. The barrier is what stops the third party — the caterer, the ice crew, the contractor with a cable — from arriving at the open door while you are inside it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Account for everybody | Select | The room is the only place in the building the release can be, so the only question that matters is whether anyone is in it. That is answered off the board before entry, because the answer changes the job from a repair into a rescue. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Read the room concentration | Graded reading | The number decides the protection. Ammonia announces itself long before it hurts you, so a reading in the low hundreds is a leak to be worked; a reading in the thousands is a room nobody enters to do maintenance, on air or otherwise, until the ventilation has pulled it down. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Dress for the room | Sequence (strict order: SCBA on air, ammonia-rated suit, gauntlets and face shield) | Air first because the pack is what you are protecting; the suit goes over it so nothing can snag the harness. The gauntlets are for liquid, not vapour — anhydrous ammonia takes the water out of skin on contact, and the burn it leaves is a cold burn that keeps going. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Enter with the ventilation running | Select | It closes behind you because it is meant to. Nothing about the entry defeats the room's containment, and the way back out is a door handle, not a wedge. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Find the leak and what it is telling you | Find (any order: the weeping shaft seal, the frosted suction line, oil under the compressor) | The seal is the leak, but the frost line and the oil are the reason the seal went: a machine flooding back has been running wet, and a wet machine washes the oil film off the seal faces. Fix the seal only and you change it again next month. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Close the king valve | Turn | The king valve is the top of the circuit you are about to empty: shut it and the receiver stops feeding the low side, so everything the compressor pulls out has somewhere to go and nothing comes back. A valve left part-closed is a valve still feeding it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Pump the low side down | Tracked hold | Steady, because a pump-down that is rushed drags liquid and oil back through a machine that is already damaged, and one that is too slow leaves the room breathing the leak for longer than it has to. The rate is the one thing the operator controls here. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Stop above atmospheric | Graded reading | Slightly positive, never into vacuum. A system left above atmospheric leaks outward if it leaks at all; one pulled into vacuum draws air and moisture in through every joint, and neither of those comes back out without a purge. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Valve the machine in, then kill the power | Sequence (strict order: suction stop valve, discharge stop valve, motor disconnect) | The valves come first so the machine is a sealed box before it is a dead box: close the electrics first and you are working the valves on a machine that a control call could still try to start. Suction before discharge, so what little charge is left is pushed forward rather than trapped behind you. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Lock the disconnect | Select | Your lock, your name. An ice plant runs on automatic controls and a building management system that has no idea your hands are inside a compressor — the lock is the only thing in the room that outranks a call for cooling. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Change the shaft seal | Select | The faces come out together and go back together: a new seal on a scored shaft sleeve is a new leak on a slower timer. What the shaft looks like under the old seal is the evidence for whether the flooding back has been going on longer than this callout. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 15 | Return it in the right order | Sequence (strict order: your lock off the disconnect, discharge stop open, suction stop open, king valve open) | Discharge before suction, always: a compressor started against a closed discharge stop has nowhere to put what it is moving, and it finds out in about a second. The lock comes off first because nothing gets opened while your lock is still on it, and the king valve last because that is what puts liquid back into a circuit you want proven tight first. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 16 | Walk the room before you sign it off | Find (any order: relief vent line, detector head, eyewash and drench shower) | The three things that will not be there when they are needed unless somebody looked today: somewhere for the relief to go, something to notice the next leak, and water for the person who is standing in it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `water-hose` | You pulled the hose to wash the leak down. Ammonia dissolves in water almost without limit, which is exactly the trap: water played onto liquid ammonia hands it the heat it needs to boil, so the pool you were trying to knock down leaves as vapour instead, and what is left is a large volume of contaminated water that is now somebody else's problem downstream. Water goes on people, or into a fog curtain a trained crew sets up. It does not go on the liquid. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `prop-door` | You wedged the machinery room door open. That door is self-closing and tight-fitting because the room is designed to hold what is in it and vent it to one known place. Propped, the room's ventilation pulls from the corridor instead, and the corridor is where everybody leaves by. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `no-scba` | You went into an alarmed machinery room without air. Ammonia gives you plenty of warning — you will smell it far below the level that hurts you, which is the one mercy of the stuff — but a release big enough to put the detector into high alarm is far past warning, and at that concentration one breath closes your airway. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `vacuum-pull` | You kept pumping after the gauge reached atmospheric. Below that, the low side draws air and moisture in through every fitting that was only ever sealed against pressure from the inside. The water makes the system corrosive and the air is a non-condensable that never leaves until somebody purges it — and in a room full of ammonia, air in the system is the other half of a flammable mixture. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

# Construction & Structural Trades

## Steel Erector (SmartCiti.X · `steel-erector`)

**Category:** Construction & Structural Trades  
**Trade:** Ironworker / structural steel connector  
**Certification / standard claimed:** Ironworkers (IW) — OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart R qualified connector; fall protection under ANSI Z359 and rigging signals per ASME B30.5  
**Tagline:** Structural steel connecting: fall protection, tag-line control and the bolt-up sequence  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the erection plan | Select | OSHA's steel erection standard, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart R, requires the erector to follow the controlling contractor's site-specific erection plan because a multi-story frame is only as stable as whatever bracing is actually in place at that moment. The raising gang works one pick at a time in the sequence the engineer set — skip ahead and the next member lands on steel that was never designed to carry it unbraced. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Connect to the horizontal lifeline | Select | ANSI/ASSP Z359 fall protection standards and OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M both start from the same fact: a connector working the leading edge of unfinished decking has nothing else rated to arrest a fall. The horizontal lifeline is anchored and inspected before the shift starts precisely so it is already load-rated before anyone needs it to work — clipping in after you are already out on the beam is clipping in one step too late. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Inspect the harness and positioning lanyard | Select | A connector's fall arrest harness will not announce webbing that has taken a shock load, a D-ring that is bent, or a lanyard shock pack that has already deployed — the damage stays invisible until the moment it is asked to catch a real fall. OSHA 1926 Subpart M treats a pre-use inspection as part of using the equipment, not an optional extra, because steel connecting is exactly the trade where a bad harness gets found out by falling in it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Confirm crane signal protocol | Select | ASME B30.5 governs the hand signals and radio communication a mobile crane crew works under, for one simple reason: the operator sitting in the cab cannot see the connection point where the load is landing. Every signal that moves the load has to mean the same thing to the operator, the rigger and the connector, because a load moving on a guess stops wherever the guess turns out to be wrong. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Scan the deck for hazards | Find (any order: unmarked deck opening, cracked temporary plank, loose decking sheet) | A deck that looks finished from the ladder is not the same thing as a deck that has been walked and checked — that is the whole logic behind requiring a hazard scan before anyone crosses a new section. OSHA's steel erection standard treats an unmarked opening, a damaged plank and loose decking as the three ways a floor that reads as solid turns out not to be, and the scan is what catches them before somebody's boot does. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Cover and barricade the opening | Carry and place | A hazard the scan found and nobody corrected is not a safer hazard — it is the same hole with one more person now aware of it and still not covering it. OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart R treats an unprotected floor opening as a fall hazard requiring a cover rated for the loads that might cross it, fastened down and marked, before the next trade walks that section of deck. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Guide the suspended column with the tag line | Timed hold | A suspended column swinging on a crane hook has no brakes and no sense of who is standing where — the tag line is the only thing keeping a connector's hands a rope's length from a ton of moving steel while still giving enough control to place it precisely. ASME B30 rigging practice calls for a tag line on any load that can rotate or drift, because a hand on the steel itself stops moving only when the steel does. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Land the member on the splice plate | Select | The splice plate below is machined to receive the column's base in one specific alignment, and it only tolerates that landing correctly once. Forcing a column down onto a plate it has not been squared to bends the plate before the first bolt is even started, turning a landing error into a fabrication problem nobody upstairs signed off on. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Plumb and align the column | Graded reading | Every connection erected above this one inherits whatever lean gets accepted at this column, because steel does not correct itself on the way up — it only adds error on top of error. OSHA's steel erection rule and standard ironworker practice both treat plumbing and bracing a column as the point where a lean is still a turnbuckle adjustment; wait until three more floors are landed on it and it is a structural problem instead. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Install bolts in the required order | Sequence (strict order: temporary bolt A, temporary bolt B, erection bolt) | Temporary bolts hold a connection snug while it is checked, plumbed and braced — that is their entire job, and it is a job the erection bolt cannot do, because putting it in early locks the joint before it has been verified. OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart R sets minimum bolt counts and sequencing for exactly this reason: a joint fastened out of order can look complete while still being unable to carry what the connection is rated for. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Apply final torque | Select | Final torque is a one-way operation — once a bolt is torqued to the connection's specified value in the required pattern, backing it off to fix an alignment problem means starting the joint over. IW apprenticeship practice and the erection plan both hold final torque until the minimum bolt count is in and the column already reads plumb, so torquing never has to double as a shortcut past the checks that came before it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Log the connection complete | Select | The crane hook stays on the load until the connection is logged as self-supporting, because that log is the only record the inspector and the next raising gang have that this joint was actually finished to the plan — bolt count, torque values, and who signed off on it. Releasing the hook before that record exists means trusting a connection that nobody but the connector has confirmed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `suspended-load-path` | You are standing under the load path. A suspended steel member has nothing holding it up but a sling and a hook — if either lets go, you are standing exactly where it lands. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `open-floor-hole` | That deck opening has no cover and no barricade. On a structural floor, a leading edge you cannot see coming is exactly how a fall happens on a surface that looks solid from three steps away. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `hand-guided-member` | You grabbed the swinging member with your hand instead of the tag line. A ton of suspended steel does not stop when your grip does — it keeps moving and takes your hand, or you, with it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `unclipped-leading-edge` | You stepped to the leading edge without your lanyard connected to the overhead lifeline. At height, the edge of unfinished decking is a fall with nothing between you and the ground below. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Crane Yard (SmartCiti.X · `crane-yard`)

**Category:** Construction & Structural Trades  
**Trade:** Mobile crane operator / rigger  
**Certification / standard claimed:** IUOE — NCCCO Mobile Crane Operator certified  
**Tagline:** Mobile crane pick: outrigger setup, load chart verification, anti-collision zone programming and a tag-line controlled lift  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the lift plan | Select | Every control that follows is sized to this specific pick, and OSHA's cranes rule at 29 CFR 1926 subpart CC puts the plan on the crew before the machine is set, not on the office afterwards. A lift plan read once the outriggers are already down is a plan you are checking your own work against. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Extend and set the outriggers | Sequence (any order: front outriggers, rear outriggers) | Rated capacity is published for beams fully extended onto adequate blocking. Retract them part way and the tipping axis moves in toward the boom, so ASME B30.5 treats that as a different chart entirely — one most cabs do not carry. The outriggers are what turn a number on paper into something this ground can hold. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Check the crane is level | Graded reading | A crane that is off level derates in the direction of the lean without saying so. Manufacturers publish their charts for a machine level within about one percent of grade, and a long boom leaning three degrees can shed a double-digit percentage of its rating — this is where you prove it rather than assume it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Verify the load chart for this pick | Graded reading | The chart is read at the actual radius and boom angle for this pick, not the radius from last week's job that felt about the same. Capacity falls away faster than radius grows, so walking the boom out a few feet can cost a fifth of the rating — and under 29 CFR 1926 subpart CC the chart, not the operator's feel for it, is the limit. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Teach the anti-collision boundary | Sequence (strict order: boundary corner A, boundary corner B, boundary corner C) | The RCI's anti-collision system only knows about a boundary you actually taught it, and it joins the points in the order it received them. Teach the corners out of order and it draws the line through the wrong side of the property — the boom then stops where nothing is and swings freely through the place you thought was fenced. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Save the boundary to the RCI | Select | A taught boundary sitting unsaved is just where the boom happened to point, and it is gone the next time the machine is keyed off. Saving it is what makes the rated capacity indicator actually cut the swing at that line, instead of leaving it to an operator remembering a property line at the end of a twelve-hour shift. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Test-swing and verify the cutout | Timed hold | An operational aid is only a control once it has been proved to act, which is why ASME B30.5 has you function-test limiting devices rather than assume them. Verifying a brand-new zone at slow test speed means the first time it stops the boom is a test, not a pick with a load hanging off the hook. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Select the correctly rated sling | Select | A sling's tag capacity assumes it is undamaged. ASME B30.9 requires an inspection before every use and lists kinks, broken stitching, heat damage and a missing tag as remove-from-service conditions — the rack always has more than one option, and the rated, sound one is the only correct choice. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Inspect the shackle | Select | A shackle with a worn or bent pin can walk loose under a cyclical load, and ASME B30.26 puts the removal criterion at roughly a tenth of the original diameter worn off the pin or the bow. The stamp tells you what it was rated for; the inspection tells you whether it still is. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Measure the sling leg angle | Graded reading | Leg tension is the share of the load divided by the sine of the angle from horizontal. Two legs at 60 degrees each carry about 58 percent of the load; at 45 they carry 71 percent, and at 30 each leg is carrying the whole load on its own. ASME B30.9 is why the angle gets measured, not eyeballed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Confirm the signal person protocol | Select | One qualified signal person directs the lift and the operator moves on that person's signal alone — with one exception written into 29 CFR 1926 subpart CC: a stop signal from anybody on the site has to be obeyed. Everyone on the pick needs to know who is calling it before the load leaves the ground. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Hook the rigging to the load | Select | The hook has to come over the load's centre of gravity before anything is taken up. A load hooked off centre swings the instant it clears the ground and puts a side pull into a boom rated only for a vertical one — and that is the moment you have least control over either. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Guide the lift with the tag line | Tracked hold | A tag line steers a suspended load without anybody putting a hand on it, and it only works at a steady light tension. Haul on it and you drag the load off plumb into a side load the boom is not rated for; let it go slack and the load keeps whatever swing it already had until something stops it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Make a controlled set-down | Carry and place | A controlled set-down means the load is sitting flat and taking its own weight before any rigging comes off. Lower it fast and the slings go slack under something that is still rocking, and the rigger who steps in to unhook is doing it under a load that can still shift onto them. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 15 | Close out the lift log | Select | The lift is not finished when the load lands. What was picked, at what radius, and anything found on the pre-use inspection are the records 29 CFR 1926 subpart CC expects to exist, and they are what the next crew and the next annual inspection work from. Rigging recovered, area confirmed clear, then logged. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `swing-radius-stand` | You are standing inside the crane's swing radius while it is rigged for a pick. The counterweight sweeps that space at walking pace with no warning a person on foot can react to, which is why OSHA's cranes rule at 29 CFR 1926 subpart CC makes barriering the swing radius the employer's job rather than the pedestrian's. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `two-block-risk` | You are hoisting past the anti-two-block limit. Running the hook block into the boom tip parts the hoist line or buckles the tip section, and the load falls the moment either one lets go — which is why ANSI/ASME B30.5 and the OSHA rule both put an anti-two-block device on the required list rather than the optional one. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `chart-exceeded` | That pick is logged past the chart's rated capacity for this radius and boom angle. A mobile crane's chart already has its safety factor built in, so the plate is the limit and not a target: cranes tip or fail structurally at the edge of the chart, not with a comfortable margin of warning first. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `kinked-sling` | That sling has a visible kink in its body. A kink is a stress concentration the sling was never rated for, and ASME B30.9 lists it as a remove-from-service condition precisely because the sling lets go at the kink well under its tag capacity. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Trench Box (SmartCiti.X · `trench-box`)

**Category:** Construction & Structural Trades  
**Trade:** Laborer / excavation and shoring  
**Certification / standard claimed:** LIUNA — OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Competent Person  
**Tagline:** Excavation shoring: competent-person inspection, atmosphere testing and protective systems  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Guard the excavation | Sequence (any order: cone at the approach, cone at the far end, trench guard rail) | MUTCD-compliant cones and the trench guard rail go up before the competent-person inspection even starts, because an open excavation next to foot traffic or a work-zone travel lane is a hazard to everyone who is not on this crew — the public does not know where the edge is until something marks it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Read the excavation permit | Select | The excavation permit sets the protective system for this trench from its actual soil classification and depth under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P — not from what looked adequate on the last job, because two trenches at the same depth in different soil do not carry the same risk of collapse. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Complete the competent-person inspection | Find (any order: tension crack at the edge, water seeping from the wall, sloughing soil face) | OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P requires a competent person to inspect the trench daily and after any event that could affect stability — rain, a freeze-thaw cycle, nearby vibration — because a wall that read as stable at the start of the shift is not guaranteed to still be the one you are standing next to now. NIOSH's trenching fatality data shows collapse gives almost no warning once a tension crack or a wet, sloughing face has already appeared. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Set the spoil pile back from the edge | Select | Spoil piled at the edge adds surcharge load exactly where the wall is already carrying the most stress, and OSHA's excavation standard sets the two-foot setback for that reason, not as a tidiness rule. Setting the pile back removes that extra weight from the equation entirely, before the wall has to hold both the soil it already had and the pile stacked on top of it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Test the trench atmosphere | Graded reading | A trench can fill with oxygen-deficient or toxic air from a nicked utility line with no smell and no colour to warn anyone first, which is exactly why OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P requires testing before every entry, not just the first one of the day — a nicked line or a change in groundwater can turn a trench's atmosphere hours after it was last checked clean. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Place the trench box | Carry and place | The trench box is rated for this depth and soil class from the permit, and OSHA's excavation standard treats it as protection that has to already be in place before anyone works below grade — not a precaution added afterward, once someone is already standing in an unshored trench hoping the wall holds through the shift. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Place the access ladder | Carry and place | A ladder within 25 feet means an exit is never more than a few steps away, in the trench or on the surface, in an emergency that gives no time to walk further. OSHA's excavation rule sets that 25-foot distance because a means of egress that exists somewhere on the job site is not the same protection as one that exists where the entrant actually is when the wall or the atmosphere turns on them. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Maintain contact with the spotter | Timed hold | The spotter watches the walls, the spoil pile and the surrounding area the whole time an entrant below grade cannot, because attention down there is on the pipe, not the edge. NIOSH lists struck-by equipment and cave-in among the leading causes of excavation deaths, and a spotter in constant contact is what catches the first one before it turns into the second. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Complete the utility line repair | Select | The actual repair only starts once guarding, inspection, atmosphere testing and shoring are all already in place — never run in parallel with them to save time, because every one of those steps exists to make the trench safe to be inside of, and none of them protects the minutes before it was actually finished. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Teach the GPS grade-control waypoints | Sequence (strict order: Start waypoint, Mid waypoint, End waypoint) | The automated grader follows these waypoints in the order they are recorded, not the order that seems obvious, so teaching start, then mid, then end has to match the pipe's actual slope. A profile taught out of order does not fail loudly — it just cuts the wrong grade the first time the machine runs it unattended over ground the crew has already left. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Save the grade-control profile | Select | An untaught point list is just three recorded positions sitting in memory, not a plan the machine can act on. Saving it is what turns them into a profile the grade-control system can actually run against, and skipping the save leaves the grader with nothing to follow the next time it powers up over this trench. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Dry-run the grade-control profile | Timed hold | A brand-new profile is verified at a walk-through pace with a hand on the console, watching the whole run, before the grader ever moves unattended over a trench a crew just worked in. Releasing the hold early is exactly how a bad waypoint gets discovered by the machine cutting the wrong grade instead of by the person watching for it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 13 | Take a headcount before backfill | Select | A headcount against the crew list is what actually confirms the trench is empty — not an assumption made because the ladder looked clear from the surface. OSHA's excavation standard treats backfilling over someone still below grade as a foreseeable failure, not a freak accident, which is exactly why the count happens before the first bucket of fill goes back in. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 14 | Remove the protective box | Carry and place | The box comes out only after everyone is confirmed clear of the trench — removing protection with anyone still below grade defeats the entire point of having placed it. It comes out the way it went in, lifted clear and set down where it is not in anybody's road. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 15 | Backfill and compact | Select | Backfilling in compacted lifts, rather than dumping it back in all at once, is what keeps the surface from settling later and undoing the repair just made underneath it — a trench that reads as finished at grade today can still slump over the utility line if the fill under it was never actually compacted. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `unshored-entry` | You stepped into the trench before the protective system was placed. A cubic metre of soil weighs more than a small car, and an unprotected wall can let go with no warning at all before it happens. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `spoil-too-close` | That spoil pile is sitting right on the edge. The extra surcharge load from a pile that close is exactly what pushes a marginal trench wall past the point it can hold itself up. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `no-ladder-access` | There is no ladder within reach of this section. If the wall lets go or the atmosphere turns, everyone below grade needs an exit inside seconds, not a walk to find one. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `untested-entry` | You are entering before the atmosphere has been tested. A trench can fill with oxygen-deficient or toxic air from a nicked utility line with no smell and no colour to warn you first. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Scaffold Erection (SmartCiti.X · `scaffold-erection`)

**Category:** Construction & Structural Trades  
**Trade:** Scaffold erector / carpenter  
**Certification / standard claimed:** UBC (Carpenters) — scaffold erector qualification; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451 / 1926.454 scaffold competent person; fall protection during erection per 1926.451(g)  
**Tagline:** Frame scaffold, two lifts: ground and sills, base plates, plumb and level, tie-ins, full planking, guardrails, ladder access, green tag  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the scaffold plan | Select | The scaffold plan is the competent person's design under OSHA's 29 CFR 1926.451 and ANSI A10.8 — how high, how tied, how loaded, and what ground it assumes underneath it. Erection follows that plan on site; improvising a taller build, a different tie pattern or a heavier load than the plan calls for turns a designed structure into a guess nobody has checked. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Inspect the ground | Select | Everything above the mudsills stands on this footprint alone. Soft ground, uncompacted backfill or a low spot that will pond water settles under load once the frames go up, and a scaffold that racks toward one settling leg is carrying its weight through connections designed to go straight down, not sideways. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Set the mudsills and base plates | Sequence (strict order: left mudsill, right mudsill, base plates on the sills) | The sill spreads the leg load over the ground; the base plate sits on the sill, never on the ground or a block. In that order, so the jacks have something to stand on. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Stand the first lift | Carry and place | The first lift sets the alignment for everything stacked on it later — square, plumb and braced now is square, plumb and braced at four lifts; out of square now multiplies at every lift after. It goes onto the base plates, gets braced both sides, and nobody lets go of the frame until the braces are actually pinned, not just leaned against it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Plumb and level the first lift | Graded reading | Out of plumb at the first lift does not stay small — it doubles at the second lift and compounds at every one after that, and by four lifts up a small lean at the base has become a structure visibly leaning off the wall. The screw jacks get adjusted now, while the scaffold is one lift high, light, and still easy to move by hand. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Tie the scaffold to the structure | Timed hold | The tie is what makes this a structure fastened to the building instead of a free-standing tower carrying its own wind load — NIOSH fatality investigations into scaffold collapses keep finding the same missing element, a tie pattern that was never installed or was installed after the fact. It goes in at the first lift, torqued to the coupler figure, before a second lift raises the wind-sail height any further. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Stand the second lift | Carry and place | The second lift only goes up once the first is plumb, level and tied — stacking height onto an unchecked lift just carries the same error higher and adds weight the tie was never sized for. Coupling pins go in so the frames cannot lift off the legs below them, and braces go on both sides so the two lifts cannot rack independently of each other. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Fully plank the working platform | Sequence (strict order: outside plank, middle plank, wall-side plank) | Full planking is the only floor the crew above ever stands on — a gap wide enough to step through is a leg through the platform onto the lift below, and a plank laid but not cleated to the ledger is a plank that walks sideways the first time someone's weight shifts near its edge, dropping whoever was standing on it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Guardrails and toeboards | Sequence (any order: top rail, mid rail, toeboard) | Ten feet up, the guardrail is the fall protection. Top rail stops a person, mid rail stops a slip under it, toeboard stops the hammer going over onto whoever is below. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Fit the access ladder | Select | The ladder is how the scaffold gets used every day after it is built, not just how it gets erected once. Without a proper access point fitted before the platform opens, the first person up climbs the cross-braces because that is what is there, and every person after them learns that climbing the frames is normal, right up until a foot goes through a brace that was never meant to carry it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Competent person inspection | Find (any order: missing coupling pin) | The green tag is the competent person's signature on a claim that every connection, tie, plank and guardrail was actually checked, not assumed. The inspection is the work that has to happen before that word means anything — walking every pin, coupler and tie by hand rather than looking at the structure from the ground and deciding it looks fine. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Hang the green tag | Select | Green says built and inspected; anyone may use it. Yellow says restrictions; red says stay off. The colour at the ladder is the whole crew's instruction. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `climb-frames` | You climbed the cross-braces to reach the second lift. Braces are not a ladder; they flex, they are not spaced for feet, and the fall is onto the frames below. Access is a ladder or a stair, built in. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `untied-work` | You started planking the second lift with no tie to the structure. Two lifts of frame scaffold with no tie is a free-standing tower over its height-to-base ratio — the wind, or one person leaning, is enough. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `block-on-sill` | You set a base plate on a concrete block instead of a mudsill. Blocks crack and tip; a base plate on a tipped block puts a leg in the air and the load on the other three. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `plank-gap` | You left a plank gap over the wall side wide enough to step through. Full planking means no gap over 1 inch at the wall, and none anywhere a foot can go. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

## Concrete Pour (SmartCiti.X · `concrete-pour`)

**Category:** Construction & Structural Trades  
**Trade:** Cement mason / concrete finisher and laborer  
**Certification / standard claimed:** OPCMIA cement masons and LIUNA laborers; ACI Concrete Field Testing Technician Grade I (slump ASTM C143, air C231, cylinders C31); OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart Q concrete and masonry (1926.701 impalement protection, 1926.703 formwork); ACI 347 formwork pressure and OSHA 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica  
**Tagline:** Wall pour from a boom pump: pre-pour walk, rebar capped and forms braced, slump and air tested before the first yard, nobody under the boom, placement rate inside the form pressure, vibrated not segregated, cylinders cast, finish on the clock  
**Automated preview:** ✅ passed 11/11 checks on 2026-09-23 · **Practitioner sign-off:** ☐ pending

### Procedure as simulated

| # | Step | Kind | Rationale shown to the learner | Reviewer: correct? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read the pour card | Select | Formwork is engineered against a rate of rise, not a volume — a form rated for a wall placed one foot an hour is a different piece of engineering from the same form placed two feet an hour. The card carries that number, the mix design and the temperature window the pour is allowed in, and none of it is negotiable on site. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 2 | Walk the pour before the truck arrives | Find (any order: uncapped vertical rebar, unpinned form brace, debris in the form) | Everything found on this walk is a five-minute fix with no truck on site and no clock running. The same defects found once concrete is moving are a stopped pour, a cold joint that never fully bonds, or somebody in the ambulance — the walk is what a five-minute fix looks like instead. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 3 | Correct what the walk found | Sequence (any order: rebar caps fitted, brace pinned, form blown out) | A defect found on the walk and left uncorrected is worse than one nobody ever spotted, because now the whole crew believes the walk happened and the form is safe to work around, when the only thing that actually happened is somebody wrote it down. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 4 | Slump test the first truck | Graded reading | Slump is the one field check that the mix arriving on the truck is the mix that was actually ordered. Too stiff and it will not fill the form around the rebar and embeds; too wet means water was added on site after batching, and water added on site is strength taken back out of the cylinder that gets broken in twenty-eight days. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 5 | Air content and cylinders | Sequence (strict order: air content measured, test cylinders cast) | Entrained air is the microscopic space that lets water expand when it freezes without cracking the paste around it, so it is what this wall survives its first winter on; the cylinders are the only proof of strength anyone will have until they are broken at twenty-eight days. Both come off the same load, before a yard of it gets placed. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 6 | Clear the boom zone | Select | The zone under a charged line is the one place on this whole pour nobody has a reason to be standing. A plugged line clears as a whip with enough force to kill, and it lets go the instant the pressure finally breaks the plug — never when anyone is watching for it, which is exactly why the zone is cleared before the line goes live, not monitored while it is. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 7 | Place the first lift | Tracked hold | The rate of rise is the number that sets the actual pressure the fresh concrete puts on the form, independent of how much has gone in total. Placing fast in one corner builds pressure there faster than the form was designed for, and a blown wall form buries whoever is standing in the pour line under tonnes of wet concrete with no warning at all. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 8 | Consolidate the lift | Timed hold | Vibration drives entrapped air out of concrete that would otherwise cure full of voids; run it too long or drag it sideways and it drives the heavy aggregate down while the cement paste rises, which is segregation and it does not un-mix once the concrete sets. Straight in, straight out, at each insertion point, and never used to push concrete sideways along the form. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 9 | Set the construction joint key | Turn | The key is the physical interlock that makes tomorrow's lift act as one structural wall with today's, instead of two slabs stacked on a plane with nothing but friction holding them. It only works pressed in while this lift is still plastic, and the surface still has to be roughened and cleaned before the next pour goes on it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 10 | Wait out the bleed water | Graded reading | Finishing while bleed water is still sitting on the surface works that same water back down into the top inch of the slab, and the top inch is the part that carries traffic and has to last decades. Trying to trowel a wet sheen away is the single most common way an otherwise good pour gets a weak, dusting surface. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 11 | Float, edge and cure | Sequence (strict order: bull float, edger and jointer, curing applied) | Curing is not cleanup at the end of the job, it is the last structural step in making the concrete: a slab that dries out in open air instead of curing under cover loses a large share of its design strength and craze-cracks across the whole surface, which no amount of good placement or vibration upstream can fix afterward. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| 12 | Cut the hardened spill wet | Carry and place | Cutting hardened concrete dry throws respirable crystalline silica into the air at many times the permissible exposure limit, in particles fine enough to reach deep into the lungs and never come back out. Water on the blade or a vacuum shroud is not a nicety, it is the entire difference between an afternoon's nuisance dust and a disease with no cure. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |

### Seeded hazards (unsafe actions)

| Hazard | Consequence shown to the learner | Reviewer: realistic? |
|---|---|---|
| `under-the-boom` | You stood under the pump boom with the line charged. A plugged line clears as a whip: the hose end swings hard enough to kill, and the plug lets go without warning when the pressure finally breaks it. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `uncapped-rebar` | You worked over uncapped vertical rebar. A fall of any height onto an uncapped bar is an impalement; the caps are rated for it and they cost less than the ambulance. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `overfill-forms` | You kept placing after the forms started to bow. Formwork fails all at once, not gradually, and it buries whoever is inside the pour line under tonnes of wet concrete. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
| `dry-cut-silica` | You dry-cut the hardened spill with no water and no vacuum. Cutting concrete dry puts respirable crystalline silica in the air at many times the permissible limit, and silicosis does not get better. | ☐ yes ☐ no — |
